title: Divisibility, factors and remainders
objective: Use divisibility tests, remainders, HCF and LCM to solve number-system questions without long division.
explanation: Every integer can be written as divisor x quotient + remainder, where 0 <= remainder < divisor. Divisibility tests are shortcuts for checking whether the remainder is zero. For two positive integers, HCF is the largest common factor and LCM is the smallest common multiple; their product equals the product of the numbers.
analogy: Think of packing items into equal boxes. The number of full boxes is the quotient, and the unpacked items are the remainder. HCF is the largest box size that fits both piles exactly; LCM is the first pile size both box patterns can reach together.

workedExamples.title: Remainder after division
workedExamples.problem: Find the remainder when 100 is divided by 3.
steps: Find the largest multiple of 3 below 100: 3 x 33 = 99.
Check that 1 is less than the divisor, 3.

workedExamples.title: HCF and LCM together
workedExamples.problem: Find the HCF and LCM of 36 and 60.
steps: Prime factors: 36 = 2^2 x 3^2 and 60 = 2^2 x 3 x 5.
HCF takes the lowest power of each common prime: 2^2 x 3 = 12.
LCM takes the highest power of every prime: 2^2 x 3^2 x 5 = 180.

rule.title: Divisibility by 3 or 9
rule.detail: Add the digits. The number is divisible by 3 or 9 when that digit sum is divisible by 3 or 9.

rule.title: Divisibility by 4 or 8
rule.detail: Check the last two digits for 4 and the last three digits for 8.

rule.title: HCF x LCM
rule.detail: For two positive integers a and b, HCF(a,b) x LCM(a,b) = a x b.

rule.title: Remainder bound
rule.detail: Always check 0 <= remainder < divisor before selecting an answer.

mistakes.mistake: Using the quotient as the remainder.
mistakes.fix: The remainder is what is left after removing full groups, not the number of groups.

mistakes.mistake: Taking the highest power of every prime for HCF.
mistakes.fix: HCF uses the lowest common powers; LCM uses the highest powers.

mistakes.mistake: Ignoring the digit sum test for 9 when checking 18.
mistakes.fix: For composite divisors, test every factor, not just one of them.

memoryTip: Remainder: multiply the full groups, then subtract. HCF is the shared smallest-power recipe; LCM is the complete highest-power recipe.

practice.prompt: What is the remainder when 257 is divided by 5?
practice.answer: 2, because the last digit gives a remainder of 2 when divided by 5.

practice.prompt: Find the LCM of 12 and 18.
Is 3,141 divisible by 9?
practice.answer: Yes. The digit sum is 3 + 1 + 4 + 1 = 9, which is divisible by 9.

title: Primes, factorisation and factor counting
objective: Factorise numbers into primes, count factors quickly and use LCM and HCF reasoning on repeating-event word problems.
explanation: Every composite number breaks into primes in exactly one way, so prime factorisation is the master key for divisibility questions. To test whether n is prime it is enough to try dividing by every prime up to the square root of n. For a number written as p^a x q^b, the total number of factors is (a + 1) x (b + 1) because each prime contributes one more choice of exponent than its power. Word problems where two events repeat at different intervals and then coincide again are solved directly with the LCM.
analogy: Prime factorisation is like the ingredient list of a dish: every recipe is built from the same basic ingredients, and the combination is unique. Counting factors is counting every way to take some or all of each ingredient.

workedExamples.title: Factorising and counting factors of 84
workedExamples.problem: Write 84 as a product of primes and count how many factors it has.
steps: Divide 84 by 2 twice: 84 = 2 x 42 = 2 x 2 x 21.
Number of factors = (2 + 1) x (1 + 1) x (1 + 1) = 3 x 2 x 2 = 12.
workedExamples.answer: 84 = 2^2 x 3 x 7 and it has 12 factors.

workedExamples.title: Two blinking lights
workedExamples.problem: A red light blinks every 12 seconds and a blue light every 18 seconds. They blink together now. After how many seconds will they blink together again, and how many times does that happen within 2 minutes?
steps: Find the LCM of 12 and 18: 12 = 2^2 x 3 and 18 = 2 x 3^2, so LCM = 2^2 x 3^2 = 36.
The lights blink together every 36 seconds.
2 minutes = 120 seconds. 120 divided by 36 gives 3 with remainder 12, so the joint blinks occur at seconds 36, 72 and 108.
workedExamples.answer: They blink together every 36 seconds, which happens 3 more times within 2 minutes.

rule.title: Prime test
rule.detail: Try primes up to the square root of n; if none divide n, then n is prime.

rule.title: Factor counter
rule.detail: For n = p^a x q^b, the number of factors is (a + 1) x (b + 1).

rule.title: Repeating events
rule.detail: Events repeating every m and n seconds coincide every LCM(m, n) seconds.

rule.title: One is special
rule.detail: 1 is neither prime nor composite; 2 is the only even prime.

mistakes.mistake: Writing the factor count as a x b instead of (a + 1) x (b + 1).
mistakes.fix: Add 1 to each exponent first: 12 = 2^2 x 3 has (2+1)(1+1) = 6 factors, which are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12.

mistakes.mistake: Testing every number up to n for primality.
mistakes.fix: Testing primes up to the square root is enough: if n = a x b, one of a or b is at most sqrt(n).

mistakes.mistake: Treating 1 as a prime.
mistakes.fix: A prime has exactly two factors; 1 has only one, so it is neither prime nor composite.

memoryTip: Square-root test for primality; add 1 to each prime exponent and multiply to count factors; LCM for events that repeat together.

practice.prompt: How many factors does 36 have?
Find the LCM of 4, 6 and 9.
Is 97 a prime? Justify your answer.
practice.answer: Yes. Its square root is below 10, and checking primes 2, 3, 5 and 7 shows none divide 97.

title: Cyclicity of powers and smart remainders
objective: Find last digits and remainders of large powers using digit cycles and reduce exponents before multiplying.
explanation: The last digit of a power follows a repeating cycle determined by the base's last digit: digits 0, 1, 5 and 6 are self-copies, while 2, 3, 7 and 8 repeat in cycles of length 4. So the last digit of a^b depends only on b mod 4 (with care for the wrap when the remainder is 0, which means the fourth entry of the cycle). For remainders, reduce the base modulo the divisor first, then multiply the reduced parts; powers modular arithmetic keeps every intermediate number small.
analogy: Units-digit cycles are clock hands: a base hand sweeps rounds of 1 or 4 positions, so only the remainder of the exponent matters, never its size.

workedExamples.title: Last digit of a big power
workedExamples.problem: Find the last digit of 3^43.
steps: Take the third entry of the cycle: 7.

workedExamples.title: Remainder by reduction
workedExamples.problem: Find the remainder when 17^2 is divided by 5, and hence when 17^200 is divided by 5.
steps: 200 mod 4 = 0, which reads as the fourth entry of the cycle: 1.

rule.title: Exponent modulo
rule.detail: For a cycle of length 4, use exponent mod 4; a remainder of 0 means the last (fourth) cycle entry.

rule.title: Base reduction
rule.detail: (a mod m)^n mod m = a^n mod m; always shrink the base first.

rule.title: Product mod m
rule.detail: Remainder of a product = product of remainders, reduced again after multiplying.

mistakes.mistake: Reading exponent mod 4 = 0 as the first cycle entry.
mistakes.fix: Remainder 0 means the cycle has completed full turns, so pick the last entry of the cycle.

mistakes.mistake: Multiplying huge powers before reducing.
mistakes.fix: Reduce the base modulo m first; 17 mod 5 = 2 keeps work tiny.

mistakes.mistake: Mixing the units-digit cycle with a remainder cycle.
mistakes.fix: Units cycles are modulo 10 only; other divisors need their own cycles.

memoryTip: Cycle length 4 for 2, 3, 7, 8; pick cycle[exponent mod 4] with 0 meaning cycle[4]; reduce bases before raising.

practice.prompt: Find the last digit of 7^100.
practice.answer: 1. Cycle 7, 9, 3, 1; 100 mod 4 = 0, so the fourth entry is 1.

practice.prompt: Find the remainder when 24^5 is divided by 7.
practice.answer: 5. Reduce the base: 24 mod 7 = 3, and 3^5 = 243; 243 mod 7 = 5 because 242 = 7 x 34.

title: Base systems, factorial zeros and combined remainders
objective: Convert between number bases, count trailing zeros in factorials and combine remainder and cyclicity tools on mixed questions.
explanation: Numbers in base 10 can be rewritten in any base b by repeated division, recording remainders from bottom to top; binary questions reverse this weighting powers of 2. Trailing zeros of n factorial count the factors of 10 available, each 10 = 2 x 5, and fives are scarcer: Z = floor(n/5) + floor(n/25) + floor(n/125) + ... . When a question mixes remainders with cyclicity, reduce the base modulo the divisor, find the exponent's position in the cycle and finish with one modular multiplication step.
analogy: Base conversion is rewriting a route in different unit stops; factorial zeros count how many times the number 10 sneaks into a gigantic product, tracked through fives rather than twos.

rule.title: Base conversion
rule.detail: Divide repeatedly by the base and read remainders upward; or expand in descending powers.

rule.title: Factorial zeros
rule.detail: Trailing zeros = sum of floor(n/5^k) over k = 1, 2, 3 ... because fives are the scarce factor.

rule.title: Combined remainders
rule.detail: Reduce base first, then use the exponent's cycle position; never multiply unreduced large powers.

rule.title: Divisibility of composites
rule.detail: For composite divisors such as 18, test every prime factor chain, not just one of them.

mistakes.fix: 25 contributes a second five: 100! needs 20 + 4, not 20.

mistakes.mistake: Reading bits right to left with ascending powers.
mistakes.fix: The leftmost bit carries the largest power of 2.

mistakes.mistake: Mixing base-10 digits into a base-b expansion.
mistakes.fix: Every digit in base b must be below b.

memoryTip: Read bits by powers of 2 descending; zeros come from fives (floor stairways of 5^k); reduces first, cycle second.

title: Digit sums, Euler-style cycles and expert remainders
objective: Classify divisibility through digit sums, deploy cycle lengths of composite remainders and combine tools for multi-step remainder questions.
explanation: Two expert-grade tools settle most remainder work. First, digit sums give divisibility by 9 (and 3): a number equals its digit sum modulo 9, so 87654321 with digit sum 36 is a multiple of 9. Second, powers of a base modulo a composite divisor also cycle, and the cycle length divides patterns visible in small powers: for example 2^6 = 64 = 9 x 7 + 1, so powers of 2 mod 9 repeat with cycle length 6, and any exponent that is a multiple of 6 returns remainder 1. Chaining both tools keeps enormous exponents manageable.
analogy: Digit sums are a referee who only counts modulo 9, and remainder cycles are Ferris wheels again: same cabin rhythm, but the wheel now rotates with a length set by the divisor.

workedExamples.title: Cycle of 2 mod 9
workedExamples.problem: Find the remainder when 2^90 is divided by 9.
steps: The cycle length is 6: any power whose exponent is a multiple of 6 gives remainder 1.

workedExamples.title: Digit-sum divisibility
workedExamples.problem: Without dividing, decide whether 87654321 is divisible by 9.
steps: A number is divisible by 9 exactly when its digit sum is.
workedExamples.answer: Yes, 87654321 is divisible by 9 (equal to 9739369 x 9).

rule.title: Digit sum mod 9
rule.detail: A number and its digit sum leave the same remainder on division by 9; the same holds mod 3.

rule.title: Cycle detection
rule.detail: Find the first exponent k where base^k leaves remainder 1; the exponent mod k locates the answer.

rule.title: Split composites
rule.detail: For a composite divisor, remainders can be confirmed through each prime power.

rule.title: Reduce early
rule.detail: Reduce both base and intermediate products modulo the divisor at every step.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming every remainder cycle has length 4.
mistakes.fix: Modulo 9 the powers of 2 cycle with length 6 (2, 4, 8, 7, 5, 1); measure the cycle, never assume it.

mistakes.mistake: Applying the digit-sum rule to divisors other than 3 and 9.
mistakes.fix: Divisibility by 11 uses alternating sums instead; each divisor has its own test.

mistakes.mistake: Reading exponent mod 6 = 0 as entry 2 or 3.
mistakes.fix: Exponent a multiple of 6 is a completed set of full turns, giving remainder 1.

memoryTip: Digit sums referee mod 9 and mod 3; find the first power giving 1 to learn the cycle length.

practice.prompt: Find the remainder when 2^50 is divided by 9.
practice.answer: 4. 50 = 6 x 8 + 2, and the cycle of 2 mod 9 is 2, 4, 8, 7, 5, 1 with length 6, so the second entry, 4, is the remainder.

practice.prompt: Is 123456789 divisible by 9?
practice.answer: Yes. The digit sum is 45, and 45 = 9 x 5, so 123456789 is divisible by 9 (indeed 13717421 x 9 = 123456789).

title: Percentage change without confusion
objective: Convert percentages into multipliers and solve increase, decrease and successive-change problems reliably.
explanation: A percentage is a fraction with denominator 100. An increase of r% multiplies by (1 + r/100); a decrease of r% multiplies by (1 - r/100). Successive changes multiply their factors in order. Reverse questions divide by the multiplier instead of subtracting a percentage from the final value.
analogy: A multiplier is a gear change. Two gear changes in a row multiply, so a 20% rise followed by a 10% fall is not a 10% rise; it is 1.20 x 0.90 = 1.08, an 8% rise.

workedExamples.problem: A price rises by 20% and then falls by 10%. What is the net change?

workedExamples.title: Reverse percentage
workedExamples.problem: After a 25% discount, a bag costs 600. What was the marked price?
steps: A 25% discount leaves 75% of the marked price.

rule.title: Increase factor
rule.detail: New value = old value x (1 + rate/100).

rule.title: Decrease factor
rule.detail: New value = old value x (1 - rate/100).

rule.title: Successive changes
rule.detail: Multiply the factors; never add the percentages directly.

rule.title: Percentage points
rule.detail: A change from 20% to 25% is 5 percentage points but a 25% relative increase.

mistakes.mistake: Adding successive percentage changes.
mistakes.fix: Multiply the growth factors instead.

mistakes.mistake: Taking a reverse percentage of the final value.
mistakes.fix: Divide by the factor that produced the final value.

mistakes.mistake: Confusing percentage points with percent change.
mistakes.fix: State the base explicitly before calculating.

memoryTip: Turn every percentage into a multiplier first. Multiply forward; divide backward.

practice.answer: No. 1.10 x 0.90 = 0.99, so it is 1% lower.

title: Percentages as fractions and percent change
objective: Convert between fractions, decimals and percentages and calculate percentage increases, decreases and discounts.
explanation: A percentage is a fraction with denominator 100, so 35 percent means 35/100 of the whole. Converting fluently between common fractions and percentages, such as 1/8 = 12.5 percent, saves time in exams. A percentage change is always computed on the original value: percent change = change divided by original, times 100. When two changes happen one after the other, they multiply as factors; for example a rise of a percent followed by a fall of a percent does not cancel to zero.
analogy: Think of percentages as a shared language for every ratio: exam marks, discounts and interest all speak it, which is why converting any ratio to parts per 100 makes different situations comparable.

workedExamples.title: Percentage change

rule.title: Basic conversion
rule.detail: x percent of y = x/100 y and x percent of y = y percent of x.

rule.title: Percent change
rule.detail: Percent change = (new - old)/old x 100, always taken on the original value.

rule.title: Successive changes
rule.detail: Multiply the factors: +20 percent then -20 percent gives 1.2 x 0.8 = 0.96, a net fall of 4 percent.

mistakes.mistake: Computing the percentage change on the final value instead of the original.
mistakes.fix: Change from 250 to 200 is 50/250 = 20 percent, not 50/200 = 25 percent.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming +x percent followed by -x percent returns to zero.
mistakes.fix: The two changes act on different bases, so they multiply as (1 plus) x (1 minus) factors.

mistakes.mistake: Confusing 'percentage of' with 'percentage more than'.
mistakes.fix: 40 percent of 60 is 24, but 40 percent more than 60 is 84.

memoryTip: Percent means out of 100; change is always measured against the starting value; successive changes multiply.

title: Successive changes and reverse percentage
objective: Compose multiple percentage changes into one net factor and reverse a percentage change to restore the original value.
explanation: Every percentage change multiplies the current value by a factor, so n successive changes compose by multiplication: +a percent then -b percent leaves the value times (1 + a/100)(1 - b/100), and the net change is read off the product. Reversing is division: if a value is the original times (1 +- r/100), then the original is the new value divided by that factor, and the common error of adding or subtracting the percentage from the new value overcorrects because the base changed.
analogy: Two successive changes are two exchange-rate hops: multiply the rates for the journey, and to find where you started, divide by the same combined rate, never re-apply it backwards.

rule.title: Compose factors
rule.detail: Multiply (1 +- r1/100)(1 +- r2/100)... and read the net percent from the product.

rule.title: Reverse by division
rule.detail: Original = final / (1 +- r/100).

rule.title: Order independence
rule.detail: Successive multiplications commute; +20 then -25 equals -25 then +20.

rule.title: Break-even pair
rule.detail: A rise of r percent is undone by a fall of 100r/(100 + r) percent.

mistakes.fix: +20 then -25 is not -5 percent; the correct net is -10 percent.

mistakes.mistake: Reversing a discount by adding the same percentage to the sale price.
mistakes.fix: 960 plus 20 percent is 1152, not 1200; divide by 0.80 instead.

mistakes.mistake: Ignoring which value the second change bases on.
mistakes.fix: After the first change, the base is the new value, so all factors chain multiplicatively.

memoryTip: Chain factors multiply; undo by dividing; a percent rise and an equal percent fall never cancel.

title: Fraction chains, populations and exam thresholds
objective: Combine fractional equivalents into multi-step percent changes and solve threshold questions with negative marking or pass marks.
explanation: Harder percent questions chain fractional equivalents like 1/4 + and 1/3 - across different bases, so every step must multiply the running value, never add fractions of different bases. Population-style questions treat each period as a compounding step; exam threshold questions set up a linear inequality of marks with optional negative marking, where the pass mark p and questions solved q must satisfy marks >= threshold. Reading whether each given percent applies to the original or the current value decides the whole answer.
analogy: Compounded bookkeeping: each percent is a transaction on the running balance, and thresholds are the minimum balance the account must end above.

rule.detail: +(r/(100 + r) percent fall) undoes an r percent rise exactly.

memoryTip: Multiply every step; complement pairs cancel exactly; thresholds are linear inequalities in marks.

title: Invalid votes, election margins and belt-type problems
objective: Solve layered percentage word problems such as election vote pools, selection filters and population pyramids.
explanation: Expert percentage problems layer a whole before percents apply: an election's total votes contain invalid votes, and percents then live on the valid pool only. The method is a strict pipeline: compute each denominator first (total, valid, weight-class), then apply the stated percentages to the correct pool, and finally re-express the wanted comparison, such as a margin, on the pool named by the question. Population and selection problems follow the same shape with filters replacing invalid votes.
analogy: Layered percentage problems are sieves: the raw stream enters at the top, every filter removes its stated share, and each later percent is weighed out of whatever reached that sieve.

title: Profit, loss and discount in one framework
objective: Relate cost price, marked price, selling price and discount, and compute profit percentages from the correct base.
explanation: Profit equals selling price minus cost price; loss is the reverse. Profit percentage is normally calculated on cost price, while discount is calculated on marked price. A useful chain is: marked price -> discount -> selling price -> profit or loss against cost price.
analogy: The marked price is the label, the discount is the price cut, and the selling price is what actually reaches the till. Profit compares that till amount with what the shop paid.

title: Cost price, selling price and discount
objective: Compute profit, loss and discount percentages from cost price, selling price and marked price.
explanation: Cost price (CP) is what the seller pays to acquire an item, selling price (SP) is what it is sold for, and marked price (MP) is the printed price before any discount. Profit and loss percentages are always computed on the cost price, while discounts are always computed on the marked price. The chain is: discount is cut from the marked price to reach the selling price, and profit or loss is the gap between selling price and cost price measured on the cost price.
analogy: Think of a train journey: marked price is the full platform, the discount is the coach you lose at the start, and profit is how much further you end up past the cost-price station.

workedExamples.title: Profit percentage
workedExamples.problem: A trader buys a clock for 240 and sells it for 300. Find the profit percentage.

workedExamples.title: Discount then profit
workedExamples.problem: An article marked at 1000 is sold at a 30 percent discount. Its cost price is 500. Find the profit percentage.

rule.title: Profit on CP
rule.detail: Profit percent = (SP - CP)/CP x 100; loss percent = (CP - SP)/CP x 100.

rule.title: Discount on MP
rule.detail: Discount percent is computed on the marked price, never on the cost price.

rule.title: No profit no loss
rule.detail: When SP equals CP the profit percent is zero even if the marked price is high.

mistakes.fix: Both profit and loss percentages are defined on the cost price in exams.

mistakes.mistake: Applying the discount to the cost price.
mistakes.fix: Discount comes off the marked price; cost price is not part of that calculation.

mistakes.mistake: Subtracting percentages of different bases directly.

title: Simple versus compound interest
objective: Distinguish linear simple interest from multiplicative compound growth and apply both formulas.
explanation: Simple interest is charged only on the original principal: SI = P x R x T / 100. Compound interest charges interest on the accumulated amount, so it grows by a factor each period: A = P(1 + R/100)^T, and CI = A - P. For the same positive rate and more than one period, compound interest exceeds simple interest.
analogy: Simple interest is a straight staircase: the same height is added each year. Compound interest is a snowball: each year's interest becomes part of the next year's base.

title: Simple interest and the first years of compound interest
objective: Use SI = P r t / 100, compute compound amounts year by year, and find a rate or principal from given data.
explanation: Simple interest grows linearly: every year adds the same amount P x r/100, so SI = P r t / 100 and the final amount is P + SI. Compound interest grows geometrically: each year's interest is computed on the amount at the start of that year, so after t years the amount is P x (1 + r/100)^t. For one year the two agree; from the second year onward compound interest runs ahead, and the two-year compound interest exceeds the two-year simple interest because interest earns interest.
analogy: Simple interest is a fixed weekly allowance; compound interest is an allowance that grows because yesterday's allowance also starts paying you.

title: CI-SI gaps, rates hidden in amounts
objective: Compute the CI-SI gap for two years, recover rates or principals from amounts, and convert compounding frequencies.
explanation: For two years the compound interest exceeds the simple interest by exactly P (r/100)^2, the interest-on-interest effect; this identity solves countless two-year questions instantly. An amount after t years is P(1 + r/100)^t, so hidden rates come from dividing the amount by the principal and reading the power. When compounding switches to half-yearly, the yearly rate halves and the period doubles, giving factor (1 + r/200)^(2t).
analogy: SI is a straight road; CI is the same road with each year's junction boosting speed by r percent; the CI-SI gap after two years is precisely the bonus earned on the first boost.

title: Half-yearly comparisons and installment recovery
objective: Compare compounding frequencies exactly and price loan repayments made in equal annual installments.
explanation: Frequency changes shift both the rate slice and the period count: annual 8 percent over one year equals two half-year periods of 4 percent, whose factor (1.04)^2 = 1.0816 slightly exceeds 1.08; the extra 0.16 percent is the intra-year compounding bonus. Equal annual installments A of an n-year loan at rate r discount back like a reversed compound amount: each installment A paid after year k contributes A/(1 + r/100)^k to the principal it can service, so P = A(1/(1+r/100) + ... + 1/(1+r/100)^n).
analogy: An installment is a payment told to travel back in time: each year's future payment is trucked back to today at the interest exchange rate, and the trucked total equals today's loan.

title: Doubling ladders and root-of-factor rates
objective: Read rates from doubling or tripling patterns under simple and compound interest and project further growth from laddered data.
explanation: Under simple interest, doubling in t years fixes the rate as 100/t percent, because only the original principal earns. Compounding behaves differently: a sum under compound interest that multiplies by k in T years multiplies by k^(t/T) in t years, so doubling in 6 years becomes four times in 12 and eight times in 18. Reading a final amount as a clean power of the principal recovers the rate, for example an amount of 1.728 P in 3 years signals 1.2^3, that is 20 percent.
analogy: Simple interest is a flat staircase, compound interest a staircase built from copies of the same step block: climb twice as long and the height multiplies the block again.

title: Work rates add, times do not
objective: Solve combined-work and pipes-and-cisterns problems by adding rates rather than adding days.
explanation: If a person completes a job in d days, their rate is 1/d of the job per day. Working together, rates add: combined rate = 1/a + 1/b, and combined time is the reciprocal. If a pipe fills at rate f and a drain empties at rate e, the net filling rate is f - e.

title: One-day work rates
objective: Convert days into one-day work rates, add rates for people working together and convert combined rates back into days.
explanation: If a person finishes a job in d days, their one-day work is 1/d of the job. People working together contribute rates that add, so the combined one-day work of A and B is 1/a + 1/b and the time together is the reciprocal of that sum. Rates can also be avoided entirely by taking the LCM of the given days as the total number of units of work and converting everyone into units per day.
analogy: Think of each worker as a tap draining a tank. Two taps open together finish twice as fast only in rates, never by halving the individual days.

workedExamples.title: Two workers together
workedExamples.problem: A finishes a job in 6 days and B in 12 days. How long do they take together?
steps: One-day work of A = 1/6 and of B = 1/12.
workedExamples.answer: They finish the job in 4 days together.

workedExamples.title: Units method
workedExamples.problem: A completes a task in 10 days and B in 15 days. In how many days do they finish working together?
steps: Take LCM(10, 15) = 30 units of total work.
A does 30/10 = 3 units per day and B does 30/15 = 2 units per day.
Together = 5 units per day, so time = 30/5 = 6 days.

objective: Combine partial work phases, include outlets and leaks as negative rates, and convert efficiency ratios into times.

When the statement gives an efficiency ratio like A is twice as efficient as B, write rates as ratio parts and fix total time through the sum.

objective: Fold efficiency multiples into group times, account for leave phases and schedule alternating-day rosters correctly.
explanation: When several workers carry different efficiencies, convert all statements to one-day rate units and let the total work be the LCM of implied day counts; efficiency ratios then become integer rates in that unit system. title: Weekly rosters and seven-day schedules
objective: Combine efficiency data with weekly work calendars and close problems whose rates repeat every seven days.
explanation: When work follows a weekly calendar, compute one week's total contribution in work units, then advance in whole weeks and finish the remainder day by day. Take total work as the LCM of the given day counts; each worker's rate becomes an integer daily amount. Days off, joining late and assistants only rewrite the weekly sum, never the method.
analogy: A weekly roster is pension instalments: compute the weekly pension in work-units, collect whole weeks, then pay out the closing days by hand.

workedExamples.title: Five-plus-two roster
workedExamples.problem: A alone finishes a job in 15 days and B alone in 20 days. A works Monday to Friday each week; B works Saturday and Sunday. Starting on a Monday, when does the job finish?
steps: A's rate = 60/15 = 4 units per working day; B's rate = 60/20 = 3 units per working day.
One week: A gives 5 x 4 = 20 units; B gives 2 x 3 = 6 units; total 26 units.
Week 3, Monday: A works 4 units -> 56. Tuesday: 4 more -> 60, complete.
workedExamples.answer: The job finishes on Tuesday of the third week: 16 days after starting.

workedExamples.title: Late-joining helper
workedExamples.problem: Same roster, but B only starts in week 2 (Saturday of week 2). Same capacities. When does the job finish?
steps: Week 3: A 20 -> 66, but work is 60, so A alone crosses the line during Thursday-Friday.
After Monday-Thursday of week 3: 46 + 16 = 62 covers the 60, so the work ends on Thursday of week 3.
workedExamples.answer: Thursday of week 3, which is 18 days after starting.

title: Mixtures, alligation and replacement
objective: Use alligation for mixing values and track quantities when a mixture is partly replaced.
explanation: Alligation finds the ratio in which two ingredients of different values must be mixed to obtain a target value. The ratio is the cross-difference between the target and each ingredient value. For a mixture, total quantity times concentration gives the amount of each component. Replacement problems are easiest when you track the amount of one component after each removal and refill.
analogy: Alligation is balancing a see-saw around the target value. The ingredient farther from the target must be used in a smaller quantity.

title: Two-part mixtures and weighted averages
objective: Compute concentrations inside a given mixture, form weighted averages of two sources and set up the basic alligation ratio.
explanation: A mixture problem tracks the amount of each ingredient: if milk and water are mixed in the ratio 3 : 1 in 20 litres, there are 15 litres of milk and 5 litres of water. The price or strength of a mixture is the weighted average of its sources, where the weights are the quantities mixed. Alligation is the shortcut that reverses this: when two ingredients priced cheaper than the mixture, the mixing ratio equals the difference between the two farthest prices, that is (dear price - mean price) : (mean price - cheap price).
analogy: A mixture is a bank account of ingredients: every deposit adds to both the balance (quantity) and the average interest (strength), and alligation simply reads back which deposits produced a given average.

title: Dilution, strengthening and the alligation grid
objective: Handle water additions and milk removals that change concentration, and use the alligation grid to find mixing ratios and prices.
explanation: Adding water dilutes a mixture: quantities change but milk's litres are unchanged, so recompute the ratio from fixed milk over new total. Removing some mixture and replacing it carries away each ingredient proportionally, which powers the replacement formula: after repeating pour-outs of volume v from a vessel of volume V, the original component remains V x ((V - v)/V)^n. The alligation grid places the two source values left, the desired mean in the middle, and reads differences to get the mixing ratio of quantities.
analogy: Replacement is mortgage amortisation for chemistry: every repayment removes an equal share of all remaining wealth, so the original asset decays by a constant factor each round.

analogy: An equation is a balanced scale. Whatever you do to one side, do to the other. Identities are pre-built tools that save you from rebuilding the same expression.

explanation: A linear equation states that two expressions stay equal; whatever is done to one side must be done to the other. A pair of equations in two variables is solved by elimination, adding or subtracting aligned copies to cancel one variable, or by substitution, replacing one variable with an expression from the other equation.
analogy: An equation is a balanced seesaw: adding or removing equal weights on both sides keeps it level. Solving two equations is like two spies who each know one fact; elimination makes them share until one secret disappears.

title: Identities and two-variable word setups
objective: Apply the standard algebraic identities without expansion and translate word problems into two correct linear equations.
explanation: Memorised identities turn long multiplications into instant evaluations: (a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2, (a - b)^2 = a^2 - 2ab + b^2, a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b) and (a + b)^3 or a^3 + b^3 in their factorised forms. Word problems convert each sentence about totals and differences into an equation; two sentences in two unknowns give two equations, solved by elimination. title: Surds, exponents and discriminant diagnosis
objective: Simplify surd expressions, combine exponent laws cleanly and diagnose quadratic equations through the discriminant.
explanation: Exponent laws let equivalent expressions collapse: 4^(a+1) = 2^(2a+2) and 8^(a-1) = 2^(3a-3), so 2^a x 4^(a+1) / 8^(a-1) = 2^(a + 2a + 2 - 3a + 3) = 2^5 = 32, independent of a. Surds simplify by extracting perfect-square factors; unlike surds refuse to merge. For quadratics, the discriminant D = b^2 - 4ac signs the terrain: D > 0 two real roots, D = 0 a doubled root, D < 0 no real roots; roots then follow the quadratic formula.
analogy: Exponent law is one-law arithmetic for all powers of the same base: every mixed expression is an invitation to common-base bookkeeping; the discriminant is the soil test before building roots.

title: Pairwise-sum systems and symmetric shortcuts
objective: Solve systems built from pairwise sums using symmetric sums and verify with quick back-substitution.
explanation: When a system gives pairwise sums such as x + y = 10, y + z = 14 and z + x = 12, add all three: 2(x + y + z) = 36, so the grand sum S = 18. Each variable is then S minus the opposite pairwise sum: x = S - (y + z) = 4, y = S - (z + x) = 6, z = S - (x + y) = 8. This symmetric-sum trick generalises to averages, weights and totals across context problems.
analogy: Pairwise sums are three overlapping umbrella arcs; totaling them counts the middle twice, and subtracting back each arc recovers the exact spokes.

explanation: An arithmetic progression (AP) is a list in which every term is the previous term plus a fixed common difference d. title: Series arithmetic beyond the nth term
objective: Work with geometric progressions, recover series from given sums, and use special formulas for sums of evens, odds and squares.
explanation: A geometric progression (GP) multiplies by a constant ratio r; the nth term is a r^(n-1) and sums of a fixed number of terms follow S_n = a (r^n - 1)/(r - 1) when r differs from 1. The reverse skill also matters: given a sum formula S_n, the kth term is S_k - S_(k-1). title: Perimeters and areas of plane figures
objective: Compute perimeters and areas of rectangles, squares, triangles and circles, and apply the Pythagoras theorem to right triangles.
explanation: Perimeter measures the boundary length of a figure and area measures the surface it covers, so perimeter is measured in units and area in square units. A rectangle with sides l and b has perimeter 2(l + b) and area l x b; a square with side a has perimeter 4a and area a^2. A triangle has area one-half base times height, and a circle of radius r has circumference 2 x pi x r and area pi x r^2, using pi = 22/7 in exams. In a right triangle the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the legs.
analogy: Perimeter is the fence around a farm, area is the crop that fits inside; the fence follows the edge while the crop spreads over every square patch.

title: Comparative growth and percentage-point traps
objective: Compare growth rates across rows or periods, convert between percentages and percentage points and compute weighted body indexes.
explanation: Two common DI traps test careful comparison. First, growth percent depends on the base period, so a bigger absolute rise can carry a smaller percent rise. Second, percentage points and percent growth differ: moving from 20 percent to 25 percent is 5 percentage points but 25 percent growth, since 25/20 - 1 = 0.25. When several categories mix with different weights, each contributes its percent change multiplied by its weight share.
analogy: Growth on a small base is a trampoline and on a big base a ramp: same upward jump height reads completely differently once you normalise by the base.

title: Cross-table computations and index building
objective: Combine rows and columns through ratios, build weighted indexes and interpret unit-growth sequences accurately.
explanation: Advanced DI compares across two dimensions at once: entity versus period, category versus region. The reliable pattern is to compute one derived ratio per cell you need, then sum or average those ratios with weights from the table itself. Weighted indexes multiply each category's growth by its base share; unit-growth sequences chain percentages across periods, requiring base-by-base multiplication rather than simple addition.
analogy: A DI table is a woven mesh: you weave derived ratios along rows and columns, then reinforce with weights, never trusting a naked average.

title: Weighted indexes and reverse share lookups
objective: Build weighted indexes from category tables and invert shares into absolute values.
explanation: A weighted index multiplies each category's growth rate by its base share and sums: weights 40, 35 and 25 percent carrying growth of 12, 6 and 10 percent give 0.40 x 12 + 0.35 x 6 + 0.25 x 10 = 4.8 + 2.1 + 2.5 = 9.4 percent overall. The reverse skill is just as valuable: when a table gives shares and one absolute anchor, every other absolute is shares times the anchor, and checkable totals close the loop.
analogy: A weighted index is a class test with section weights: each section's average is scaled by its mark-share; reverse lookups are invoices recovered from percentage coupons plus one known price.

title: Find the rule behind a series
objective: Recognise difference, ratio, alternating, square and mixed patterns in number and letter series.
explanation: Start with first differences. If they are constant, the series is arithmetic. If the differences change in a regular way, look at second differences. If terms grow quickly, test ratios. Also check alternating operations, squares, cubes and coprime integer rules. For letter series, write the alphabet positions and test shifts.
analogy: A series is a hidden machine. Feeding the terms through candidate operations is like testing gears: difference, ratio and square patterns are the usual gearboxes.

rule.title: Ratio test

rule.title: Second difference

rule.title: Known sequences

rule.title: Letters

title: Differences and ratios in short series
objective: Identify constant-difference, constant-ratio and growing-gap patterns in short number series and find the missing term.
explanation: Most entry-level series questions use one of three patterns: a constant difference, such as +5 every time; a constant ratio, such as doubling; or a growing gap, where the differences themselves form a simple series. The standard method is to compute consecutive differences first, then ratios if differences are not constant, then look at the differences of the differences. Alternating patterns place two interleaved series side by side.
analogy: A number series is a dance: step size may stay fixed (walk), multiply (run) or grow (accelerate); reading the step size each turn identifies the dance.

rule.title: Ratios second

rule.title: Second differences
rule.detail: If first differences grow by a constant, extend the difference list one step.

rule.title: Alternating series
rule.detail: Split alternate terms into two independent mini-series.

mistakes.mistake: Reading the series backwards for a missing early term.
mistakes.fix: Work outwards from both ends and meet in the middle.

title: Reachable patterns: primes, squares-plus and interleaves
objective: Recognise prime sequences, shifted square sequences and interleaved series, then extend them correctly.
explanation: Beyond differences and ratios, several structures recur in exams: prime numbers (2, 3, 5, 7, 11, ...), squares shifted by a constant such as n^2 - 1, tables of multiplied terms hidden in plain lists, and interleaved series made of two simpler chains on alternating positions. The method is to test the classic families in order: primes, squares +/- constant, cubes +/- constant, triangular numbers and finally interleaving two free series.
analogy: Series are masked dancers at fixed meetups: squares minus one always wears the off-by-one scarf; to unmask, try the guest list of famous families first.

title: Operated chains and factorial steps
objective: Decode series built by alternate operations, factorial-based jumps and digit-plus-position rules.
explanation: Advanced series build each term by applying an operation whose operand grows: multiply by 3 then subtract 1 in every step; add 2, then 4, then 8 doubling fills; or insert factorials 1, 2, 6, 24 as jump sizes. Digit-based rules use the term's own digits, like adding the digit sum. The decoding drill: tabulate consecutive operations, look for the operand pattern (constant, doubling, multiplication), and verify across at least two transitions.
analogy: Operated chains are gearboxes with a growing input: the same gear ratio applies at each step but to a bigger number, and the operand series is the pedal cylinder.

workedExamples.title: Multiply then subtract chain
workedExamples.problem: Find the next term: 2, 5, 14, 41, ...
steps: Operations: x3 - 1 each step: 2 x 3 - 1 = 5, 5 x 3 - 1 = 14, 14 x 3 - 1 = 41.
Verify one more interior transition: correct on all three.

rule.title: Operation operand
rule.detail: Same operation with a computed operand: read its own pattern (constant, doubling, factorial).

rule.title: Factorial staircase
rule.detail: 1, 2, 6, 24, 120 jumps appear as differences or as multipliers.

rule.title: Digit rules
rule.detail: Digit sums, digit products and reversed digits can generate the next term.

rule.title: Double verification

mistakes.fix: Tabulate operands: 1, 2, 6, 24 is factorial, not noise.

mistakes.mistake: Testing rules only on the last transition.
mistakes.fix: Validate across the whole visible window.

mistakes.mistake: Overlooking digit-based rules with no arithmetic clue.
mistakes.fix: When differences and ratios both fail, inspect digits.

memoryTip: Operation plus operand: same gear, growing pedal; factorial staircases hide in difference rows; verify twice.

title: Two-row differences that breathe their own rhythm
objective: Decode series whose gaps form a secondary pattern and extend them reliably.
explanation: The gap row is a series of its own: in 2, 10, 26, 50 the gaps are 8, 16, 24, an arithmetic run with common difference 8, so the next gap is 32 and the next term 82. Two-row bookkeeping (terms row, difference row, sometimes a third) turns almost any exam series into honest arithmetic, provided the second row's own rule is verified on all visible gaps.
analogy: The difference row is the drumbeat under the melody: once the drum's own rhythm locks in, every coming bar is predictable.

title: Decode the rule, then apply it
objective: Identify letter shifts, reversals and symbol substitutions in coding questions.
explanation: Write the alphabet with positions if shifts are involved. Compare each coded letter with its original to find a constant shift, alternating shift or reversal. For word codes, check whether letters are moved forward, backward, reversed, or replaced by the next/previous letter. Apply the discovered rule consistently to the target word.
analogy: A code is a translation rule. Once you know the rule, translating a new word is mechanical; guessing a translation without the rule is unreliable.

rule.title: Alternating rules

title: Fixed-shift letter codes
objective: Encode and decode words with fixed positional letter shifts, numeric letter positions and simple reversal codes.
explanation: Coding questions map letters or numbers through one visible rule. The most common are fixed shifts, where every letter moves k positions ahead or back in the alphabet, and A1Z26 numbering, where A = 1 up to Z = 26. Reversal codes write the word backwards. Given one coded pair, compare word and code letter by letter to derive the shift, then apply the same rule consistently to the asked word.
analogy: A fixed-shift code is a Caesar wheel: every letter slides along the same rim distance; once the rim is calibrated from one pair, the wheel never moves again.

rule.title: A1Z26

rule.title: Reversal

title: Composite codes: sums, mixed shifts and reverse alphabets
objective: Decode letter-sum codes, handle alternating shifts across letters and use the reverse-alphabet mapping.
explanation: Beyond fixed shifts, three composite structures recur. Letter-sum codes replace a word's letters by the sum or list of their A1Z26 values, so calibrating needs whole-word arithmetic. Alternating-shift codes move neighbouring letters by different step sizes, typically +1 and -1 alternately. The reverse alphabet maps A to Z, B to Y and so on through the formula code = 27 - position. Each composite must be calibrated from the given pair before being applied anywhere else.
analogy: Composite codes are machines with two working gears working together: sum gears add up letters, alternation gears send neighbours opposite directions; calibrate once from a labelled pair.

rule.title: Reverse alphabet

title: Layered codes: shift plus reversal and mixed schemes
objective: Decode codes formed by two stacked rules, choose among letter-reversal, word-split and digit-letter hybrid schemes.
explanation: Advanced codes stack simple rules: first shift every letter by k, then reverse the whole word; or split the word and code the halves differently. Because stacked rules are confusing to read directly, decode in reverse order: un-reverse first, then un-shift. Hybrid schemes replace letters with their positions and recombine digits; decoding always begins by reproducing the given example's two transformations explicitly.
analogy: Layered codes are wrapped parcels: unwrap in reverse order of packing, one layer at a time, until the readable label reappears.

Shift -2 on each: V-2 = T, K-2 = I, V-2 = T, C-2 = A, P-2 = N.

rule.title: Decode backwards
rule.detail: Undo the last transformation first; layers peel in stack order.

rule.title: Split schemes
rule.detail: Words may code by halves with different shifts; identify the boundary from the example.

rule.title: Hybrid digits
rule.detail: Letter-position digits recombined still obey layer order; keep columns aligned.

rule.title: Example-first discipline
rule.detail: Never apply an unverified scheme; reproduce the given pair fully before coding the new word.

mistakes.fix: The last applied rule is the first undone.

mistakes.mistake: Applying a stacked rule unchecked on the given pair.
mistakes.fix: Verify the whole transformation pipeline on the example.

mistakes.mistake: Mixing which half takes which shift in split schemes.
mistakes.fix: Label halves explicitly from the calibration pair.

memoryTip: Peel in stack order, verify on the given pair, and keep hybrid digit columns aligned.

practice.prompt: Why must decoding peel layers in the opposite order of packing?
practice.answer: The last rule applied is the first undone; peeling in packing order mixes shifted and reversed letters.

title: Layered shift-and-reverse codes on new words
objective: Calibrate a two-layer code from a given pair, code new words and decode arbitrary outputs back to plain text.
explanation: Two-layer codes first shift letters by a constant, then reverse the whole word. Calibrating from a given pair - for example TIPS coded as WTMX under shift +4 then reversal: T + 4 = X, I + 4 = M, P + 4 = T, S + 4 = W giving XMTW, then reversing to WTMX - fixes both layers. Coding new words applies the same pipeline; decoding peels in reverse order: un-reverse, then un-shift.
analogy: A two-layer code is a wrapped parcel tied with a letter-shift stamp: pack by shifting then flipping, unpack by flipping back then un-stamping.

workedExamples.title: Calibrate then code
workedExamples.problem: Given TIPS becomes WTMX under shift +4 then reversal, encode RENT with the same scheme.
steps: Shift +4: R to V, E to I, N to R, T to X, giving VIRX.

workedExamples.title: Peel in reverse order
workedExamples.problem: Using the same scheme, decode the output MWDT back to plain text.
steps: Result letters: T D W M unshifted: P Z S I.

rule.title: Pack order
rule.detail: Shift first, reverse second: fix the order from the given pair.

rule.title: Peel order
rule.detail: Decoding un-reverses first, then un-shifts.

rule.title: Wrap handling
rule.detail: Shifting below A or above Z wraps by 26 positions.

rule.title: Verify on the given pair
rule.detail: Replicate the pair end-to-end before coding the new word.

mistakes.mistake: Reversing before shifting when the scheme says shift first.
mistakes.fix: .dtpack the example: WTMX un-reversed is XMTW, whose letters are exactly TIPS + 4.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting the wrap on D - 4.
mistakes.fix: Wrap modulo 26: D 4 becomes Z 26 after subtracting 4.

mistakes.mistake: Applying two different shift sizes for calibration and coding.
mistakes.fix: The shift constant is calibrated once and reused.

memoryTip: Pack shift-then-flip, peel flip-then-unshift; wrap letters past the alphabet ends.

practice.prompt: With shift +2 then reverse, encode MARS.
practice.answer: UTCO. Shift each letter forward by 2: M to O, A to C, R to T, S to U, giving OCTU; then reverse the string to get UTCO.

practice.prompt: Decode VOKI under the same scheme (shift +2 then reverse).
practice.answer: GIMT. Un-reverse VOKI to IKOV, then shift each letter back by 2: I to G, K to I, O to M, V to T, giving GIMT.

practice.prompt: Why does decoding peel in the opposite order?
practice.answer: Because the last transformation applied is the first undone; keeping the order right avoids mixing layers.

title: Draw the family tree
objective: Translate relationship statements into a family tree and answer generation and relation questions accurately.
explanation: Use a small set of symbols: horizontal line for siblings, vertical line for parent-child, and mark gender where stated. Work through one sentence at a time. Determine generation differences before naming the relation. Do not assume a gender from a role unless the statement makes it explicit.
analogy: A family tree is a graph. People are nodes and relationships are edges. Tracing the path from one node to another tells you the relation.

workedExamples.title: Parent through a sibling
workedExamples.problem: P is Q's mother. Q is R's brother. How is P related to R?
steps: Q is male and R is Q's sibling.
P is Q's mother, so P is also the mother of Q's sibling R.

workedExamples.title: Grandparent
workedExamples.problem: A is B's father. B is C's father. How is A related to C?
steps: A is one generation above B.
B is one generation above C.
Therefore A is two generations above C.

rule.title: Generations
rule.detail: Count vertical steps: parent-child is one generation; grandparent-grandchild is two.

rule.title: Siblings
rule.detail: Brothers and sisters share at least one parent; a sibling's parent is also your parent.

rule.title: Gender clues
rule.detail: Use only explicit words such as mother, father, brother or sister.

rule.title: Spouse links
rule.detail: Mark marriage separately; it connects generations without being a blood parent-child edge.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming every sibling is male or female from the name.
mistakes.fix: Use only the stated gender; otherwise keep the relation neutral.

mistakes.mistake: Ignoring a second marriage or half-sibling clue.
mistakes.fix: Draw each stated link explicitly.

mistakes.mistake: Naming a relation without counting generations.
mistakes.fix: Trace the path and count vertical steps.

memoryTip: Circle people, draw parent edges vertically, sibling edges horizontally, and count generations before naming the relation.

title: Two-line family statements
objective: Convert short chains of everyday family statements into relations, using tree diagrams and standard exam assumptions.
explanation: Blood-relation questions describe a family through a few statements and ask for the relation between two members. The reliable method is to draw a small tree: one row per generation, with vertical lines for parent-child and horizontal links for couples or siblings. Standard exam conventions apply: statements like spouse pairs are taken in the usual way, and no gender is ever assumed unless stated. Never infer a relation the statements do not force.
analogy: Each statement is one plank of a bridge between two people; the answer is the full walk across planks, not a leap between distant towers.

workedExamples.title: Uncle through a sibling chain
workedExamples.problem: A is the brother of B. B is the mother of C. What is A to C?
steps: Draw: A and B on the same row (siblings); C one row below B.
B is the parent of C; A is a sibling of C's parent.
A is male, so A is the uncle of C.

workedExamples.title: Parents as spouses
workedExamples.problem: P is the father of Q. Q is the daughter of R. What is R to P?
steps: Q has two parents named: father P and parent R.
Under standard exam assumptions the two parents of the same child are spouses.
So R is the wife of P.

rule.title: Draw before answering
rule.detail: A two-row sketch of generations settles most questions instantly.

rule.title: Gender discipline
rule.detail: Never assume gender; uncles, nieces and grandfathers are only males because the statement says so.

rule.title: Sibling bridge
rule.detail: Sibling of a parent is an uncle or aunt; sibling of a grandparent is a great-uncle or great-aunt.

rule.title: Spouse convention
rule.detail: Two named parents of one child are treated as a couple unless stated otherwise.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming gender from names or roles.
mistakes.fix: Only conclusions forced by stated genders are valid.

mistakes.mistake: Skipping a generation link.
mistakes.fix: Require one clear parent-child step per generation, grouped by row.

mistakes.mistake: Confusing 'brother of my mother' with 'brother of my father'.
mistakes.fix: Mark which side of the family each branch belongs to before naming the relation.

memoryTip: Rows are generations, lines are facts, and no male symbol without a stated gender.

practice.answer: Grandmother. Y is the parent of X's mother.

practice.answer: Son. Both A and B are children of C.

title: Symbol-coded relations and generation tracking
objective: Parse symbol-coded relation chains, assign genders from codes only and answer with generation bookkeeping.
explanation: Symbol codes replace words like mother of or son of with signs: each symbol carries a fixed relation and carries gender information when the family words do. Parse chains left to right, remember that every sign applies between its immediate neighbours, and draw the tree as you go. Because the final question asks across the whole chain, mark the gender of each person only when a code states it; unknown genders block gendered answers such as uncle or niece and push towards neutral words like child or parent.
analogy: Symbol chains are grammar-free sentences: each sign is a verb with fixed family meaning, and the tree you draw is the sentence's diagram, gendered only where the codes say so.

workedExamples.title: Two-symbol chain
workedExamples.problem: In a code, A @ B means A is the mother of B and A # B means A is the father of B. Parse P @ Q # R. What is P to R?
steps: P @ Q: P is the mother of Q.
Q # R: Q is the father of R.
So Q is male, R is Q's child (gender unknown), and P is the mother of R's father.

workedExamples.title: Chain with a sibling sign
workedExamples.problem: With + for brother of and - for sister of, parse A + B - C, where all symbols state genders. What is A to C?
steps: A + B: A is the brother of B (A male).
B - C: B is the sister of C (B female).
A is the male sibling of C's parent.

rule.title: Local application
rule.detail: Each symbol joins exactly the two people beside it; never read across signs.

rule.title: Gender from codes only
rule.detail: Mother, father, brother and sister codes carry gender; child, parent and cousin codes do not.

rule.title: Tree as you parse
rule.detail: Draw rows per generation immediately; the final answer reads across the tree.

rule.title: Neutral fallback
rule.detail: When gender at a link is unknown, the answer collapses to a neutral relation like child or parent.

mistakes.mistake: Reading two symbols across an unknown middle person.
mistakes.fix: Compose the relation stepwise through the middle person.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming gender of a person linked only by neutral codes.
mistakes.fix: Without gender words, uncles and nieces are unprovable.

mistakes.mistake: Mixing up in-law direction after a sibling link.
mistakes.fix: Sibling of the parent is uncle or aunt; sibling of the spouse is in-law.

memoryTip: Sign joins its neighbours; genders come only from stated words; compose stepwise along the drawn tree.

practice.prompt: Parse M - N + P with - sister and + brother. What is P to M?
practice.answer: M is female and a sibling of N, who is male and a sibling of P. M and P are siblings of the same person; gender of P is unknown, so P is M's sibling.

practice.prompt: Parse X @ Y with @ meaning 'is the mother of'; what gender is Y's parent stated here?
practice.answer: The mother side is female (X); Y's father is not mentioned.

practice.prompt: In P # Q @ R (# father, @ mother), what is P to R?
practice.answer: Paternal grandfather. P is the father of Q and Q is the mother of R.

title: Coded trees with spouses and gender closures
objective: Parse long symbol chains including spouse symbols, close gender gaps by inference and answer cross-generation questions.
explanation: Long coded chains add spouse signs alongside descent signs; a spouse link joins people horizontally on one generation row. Parsing proceeds sign by sign, drawing rows immediately, and gender can close by inference: someone who signs as father or mother is gendered, and a child linked to them inherits nothing, only a parent link. The final question often spans two or more generations, so label rows G1, G2, G3 to keep the walk honest.
analogy: Coded trees are subway maps: descent signs are vertical escalators, spouse signs are same-level corridors, and lines labelled G1, G2, G3 stop you crossing wrongly.

workedExamples.title: Three-generation chain
workedExamples.problem: Symbols: + father of, - mother of. Parse A + B - C + D. What is A to D?
steps: A + B: A is B's father (G1 to G2).
B - C: B is C's mother (G2 to G3).
C + D: C is D's father (G3 to G4).
A is the father of B, who is the mother of D's father.
workedExamples.answer: A is D's great-grandfather: three descent hops (A to B to C to D), with B as C's mother.

workedExamples.title: Gender closure
workedExamples.problem: Symbols: @ mother of, # father of. Parse M @ N # P. What is M to P?
steps: M @ N: M is N's mother.
N # P: N is P's father; so N is male.
M is the mother of P's father.

rule.title: Rows per generation
rule.detail: Label G1 downward; descent moves one row, spouses stay put.

rule.title: Closure by gendered sign
rule.detail: Father and mother symbols gender their subject directly; children inherit only links.

rule.title: Chain composition
rule.detail: Compose the final walk relation stepwise; check the direction of each hop.

rule.title: Grandparent labelling
rule.detail: Three hops give grand; four hops great-grand; say the side honestly.

mistakes.mistake: Skipping one generation while naming the answer.
mistakes.fix: Count hops: one is parent, two grand, three great-grand.

mistakes.mistake: Letting an unrelated person's gender leak into the answer.
mistakes.fix: Only gendered symbols license gendered words.

mistakes.mistake: Reading spouse symbols as descent.
mistakes.fix: Spouses share a row; no generation change occurs.

memoryTip: G-rows stop missteps; gendered signs close genders; hops count the generation distance.

practice.prompt: Parse X # Y - Z (- mother, # father): what is X to Z?
practice.answer: Grandfather. X is the father of Y, who is the mother of Z.

practice.prompt: Parse A @ B with @ mother. Gender of A?

practice.answer: Grandfather. P is the father of Q, and Q is the father of R: two descent hops.

title: Photograph puzzles and self-reference traps
objective: Solve pointing-to-photograph statements where the speaker refers to themselves through layered descriptions.
explanation: Photograph puzzles embed the speaker in the family description: a line such as the man's mother is the only daughter of my mother links through the speaker herself, because the only daughter of my mother is me when I am that daughter. Unfolding such self-references step by step - first naming the bridging description, then replacing it with the speaker - resolves which relative the speaker is to the photographed person.
analogy: A photograph puzzle is a mirror hallway: the statement reflects through the speaker, and each bounce (my mother, her only daughter) must be named before the final face is identified.

workedExamples.title: Mother in the mirror
workedExamples.problem: Pointing to a man, a woman says: His mother is the only daughter of my mother. How is the woman related to the man?
steps: The only daughter of the woman's mother is the woman herself (she is female and the description names a daughter).
So the man's mother = the woman.
The woman is the man's mother.

workedExamples.title: Father's only son
workedExamples.problem: Pointing to a photograph, a man says: She is the daughter of my grandfather's only son. How is the photographed person related to him?
steps: The grandfather's only son is the man's father.
The daughter of his father is his sister.
So the photographed person is his sister.

rule.title: Resolve bridges first
rule.detail: Translate phrases like only son or only daughter into named people before linking.

rule.title: Self-reference check
rule.detail: When the bridge is itself (the only daughter of my mother), substitute the speaker's gender before concluding.

rule.title: Gender of speaker matters
rule.detail: Fix title later

rule.title: Draw both generations
rule.detail: Sketch the two rows (speaker's parents, siblings, children) before naming the final relation.

mistakes.mistake: Reading only daughter of my mother as a sibling.
mistakes.fix: If the speaker is that daughter, the bridge is the speaker herself; verify the gender of the speaker first.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming grandfather's only son excludes the speaker's father's brothers.
mistakes.fix: Only son means the father has no brothers, so the bridge is exactly the father.

mistakes.mistake: Answering the wrong direction (how is he related to her).
mistakes.fix: Read the question's arrow; relation statements are not symmetric.

memoryTip: Name each bridge, check the speaker's gender, then walk the two-generation tree.

practice.prompt: Pointing to a boy, a man says: He is the son of my father's only son. Relation?
practice.answer: The man's father has only one son: the man himself; so the boy is the man's son.

practice.prompt: Pointing to a woman, a man says: Her mother is the only daughter of my mother. Relation?
practice.answer: The only daughter of the man's mother is the man's sister... careful: if the speaker is male, the only daughter of his mother is his sister; the woman's mother is the man's sister; so the woman is the man's niece.

practice.prompt: She is the only daughter of my grandmother's only child: a man pointing at a girl; who is she?
practice.answer: His sister? The grandmother's only child is the man's parent; its only daughter is the man's sister if the speaker's parent is that daughter... if the speaker is male and the only child's only daughter could be the speaker's sister - the standard reading gives sister.

title: Turns, coordinates and displacement
objective: Track direction changes with a compass sketch and compute shortest distance using right triangles.
explanation: Use a fixed compass: north up, east right, south down, west left. A right turn rotates 90 degrees clockwise; a left turn rotates 90 degrees anticlockwise. Track net east-west and north-south movement separately. The shortest distance from start to finish is the hypotenuse of the resulting right triangle.
analogy: Walking directions are grid moves. Moving east changes the horizontal coordinate, moving north changes the vertical one; turns only change which axis you move along next.

workedExamples.problem: A person walks 3 km east, then 4 km north. How far are they from the start?

workedExamples.title: Facing and turning
workedExamples.problem: A person faces north, turns right, then turns left. Which direction are they facing?
steps: Facing north, a right turn points east.
Facing east, a left turn points north.

rule.title: Right turn
rule.detail: Rotate 90 degrees clockwise.

rule.title: Left turn
rule.detail: Rotate 90 degrees anticlockwise.

rule.title: Opposite turn
rule.detail: Two turns in the same direction face the opposite direction.

rule.title: Shortest distance
rule.detail: Use sqrt(horizontal^2 + vertical^2) for perpendicular movements.

mistakes.mistake: Adding all distances travelled instead of finding displacement.
mistakes.fix: Track net coordinates; total path length and shortest distance are different.

mistakes.mistake: Turning relative to the page rather than the person's current facing.
mistakes.fix: Update the facing direction after every turn.

mistakes.mistake: Mixing left and right when facing south.
mistakes.fix: Draw the compass or rotate the page mentally before turning.

memoryTip: Draw north first. Move coordinates, not just distances. Shortest path is the hypotenuse.

title: Two-leg walks and quarter-turns
objective: Track short walks on north-east-south-west lines and answer where a person ends up or how far they are from the start.
explanation: Direction questions track a walker along compass directions. Keep a running coordinate: north and east increase y and x, south and west decrease them. The distance from the start is the straight displacement, often a Pythagorean pair like 3-4-5. Turns are quarter-changes: right from north is east, and two rights from north is south. Always track which way the walker is facing after each turn.
analogy: Think of the walker as a chess rook moving on invisible graph paper: the path may twist, but the final displacement is one straight rook-and-bishop shot from square to square.

workedExamples.title: A 3-4-5 walk
workedExamples.problem: A man walks 3 km north, then 4 km east. How far is he from the start?
steps: Net position: 3 km north and 4 km east.
workedExamples.answer: He is 5 km from the start, towards the north-east.

workedExamples.title: Facing after turns
workedExamples.problem: A person facing north turns right twice. Which way does she face now?

rule.title: Compass discipline
rule.detail: North up, east right, south down, west left; turn right 90 degrees clockwise.

rule.title: Pythagorean displacement
rule.detail: Perpendicular legs use a^2 + b^2 = c^2; know 3-4-5 and 6-8-10.

rule.title: Opposite legs cancel
rule.detail: 10 north then 10 south returns to the start: zero displacement.

rule.title: Facing upkeep
rule.detail: Update the facing direction after every turn; the next move follows the new direction.

mistakes.fix: 15 walked km can end 3 km from the start if the path folds back.

mistakes.mistake: Turning the map instead of the person.
mistakes.fix: Right and left belong to the walker facing their own direction.

mistakes.mistake: Ignoring the second turn's new base direction.
mistakes.fix: Two rights from north is south, not west.

memoryTip: Keep x and y counters, remember 3-4-5, turn 90 degrees with the walker not the map.

title: Multi-leg displacement and turn bookkeeping
objective: Reduce several legs with turns to one net displacement vector and answer distance and direction from the start.
explanation: Long walks with rights and lefts reduce cleanly to coordinates: keep running x (east positive) and y (north positive) totals, update the facing direction after each turn, and read the final displacement as (dx, dy). The distance from start is the hypotenuse sqrt(dx^2 + dy^2) when both components are nonzero, and the final direction is read from the signs of dx and dy. Legs in opposite directions cancel; perpendicular leftover legs form the Pythagorean pair.
analogy: Walk legs are travel invoices in credits and debits: east-west credits subtract west debits, north-south tracks separately, and the final settlement is one straight trip from origin.

rule.detail: Track x for east-west and y for north-south throughout.

rule.title: Left/right updates

rule.title: Hypotenuse finish
rule.detail: Distance = sqrt(dx^2 + dy^2); read the direction from (dx, dy) signs.

rule.title: Cancellation

title: Shadow walks, bearings and multi-person anchors
objective: Use sun-shadow directions as anchors, chain long mixed walks, and track two movers relative to a fixed point.
explanation: Advanced direction questions anchor on natural facts: the sun rises in the east, so an early-morning shadow falls to the west, and a person walking toward their shadow faces west. Long chains still reduce to dx and dy coordinates, and two-mover questions fix one walker as the reference point, converting the other's displacement into relative position. The discipline is unchanged: one facing variable, two axis totals, explicit anchor notes.
analogy: Shadow facts are free compass calibrations; once the morning map prints west, every next step chains off the same coordinates.

workedExamples.title: Shadow anchor
workedExamples.problem: In the morning, a man walks directly toward his shadow for 10 m, then turns right and walks 8 m. How far is he from the start?
steps: Morning shadows fall west, so walking toward the shadow means walking 10 m west.
Right from west heading... facing west; right turn is north; walk 8 m north.

workedExamples.title: Relative position
workedExamples.problem: A starts at the origin and walks 5 km north. B starts at the origin and walks 5 km east. Relative to A, where is B?
steps: B relative to A: subtract (0, 5) from (5, 0), giving (5, -5): 5 km east and 5 km south of A.
workedExamples.answer: B is 7.07 km south-east of A.

rule.title: Morning shadow west
rule.detail: Sunrise east casts shadows west; afternoon reverses to east.

rule.title: Facing bookkeeping
rule.detail: Update facing after every turn; direction words belong to the walker.

rule.title: Two movers
rule.detail: Fix one as origin; the other's coordinates subtract to give relative position.

rule.title: Hypotenuse finish
rule.detail: Final distance uses sqrt(dx^2 + dy^2) with signed components.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming shadows fall north at sunrise.
mistakes.fix: Shadows point away from the sun: east sun makes west shadows.

mistakes.mistake: Comparing two movers as if both started from the same facing.
mistakes.fix: Relative position is coordinate arithmetic, not facing arithmetic.

mistakes.mistake: Dropping the negative sign on westward or southward legs.
mistakes.fix: Signs feed the final sqrt and the direction wording.

memoryTip: Shadow says west in the morning; coordinates never lie; relative position is one subtraction away.

title: Four-leg displacement with a cancellation twist
objective: Reduce multi-leg walks with turns to net displacement and answer both distance and bearing.
explanation: Track axes throughout: a walker goes 8 km north, turns right and walks 6 km east, turns right again and walks 8 km south, then turns left (now facing east) and walks 4 km east. East total = 6 + 4 = 10, north total = 8 - 8 = 0, so he is 10 km due east - the cancelled north-south pair leaves a purely horizontal displacement. Turning bookkeeping: from north, right is east; from east, right is south; from south, left is east.
analogy: A walk with cancellations is a bill with paired charges and refunds: subtract paired legs on each axis and the balance tells the straight trip home.

title: Build the arrangement one clue at a time
objective: Place people in linear and circular arrangements by using definite clues before uncertain ones.
explanation: For linear arrangements, draw as many seats as named and mark left/right from the stated facing direction. For circular arrangements, fix one person to remove rotation, note whether people face the centre or outward, and remember that left/right reverses for outward-facing people. Start with extreme positions, immediate neighbours and exact distances; leave 'somewhere left/right' clues for later.
analogy: A seating puzzle is a jigsaw. Definite clues are edge pieces; place them first, then fill the gaps with relative clues.

workedExamples.title: Linear arrangement
workedExamples.problem: Five people P, Q, R, S and T sit in a row facing north. P is at the extreme left, T at the extreme right, Q is immediately to the right of P, and R is immediately to the left of T. Who is third from the left?
steps: P is seat 1; T is seat 5.
Q is seat 2; R is seat 4.
The row is P, Q, S, R, T.
workedExamples.answer: S is third from the left.

workedExamples.title: Circular positions
workedExamples.problem: Four people A, B, C and D sit around a circle facing the centre. A is opposite C and B is immediately to A's right. Who is opposite B?
steps: Place A at the top and C at the bottom, since they are opposite.
A faces the centre, so A's right points to the page-left seat (9 o'clock). Place B there.
The remaining seat at 3 o'clock belongs to D.

rule.title: Fix the frame
rule.detail: Draw all seats and mark the facing direction before placing anyone.

rule.title: Use definite clues first
rule.detail: Extremes, immediate neighbours and exact gaps are strongest.

rule.title: Circular rotation
rule.detail: Fix one person to break rotational symmetry; then positions become unique.

rule.title: Facing direction
rule.detail: Left and right are from the person's perspective, not the reader's.

mistakes.mistake: Treating a 'somewhere to the right' clue as 'immediately right'.
mistakes.fix: Only 'immediate' or 'next to' fixes adjacency.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming clockwise equals right for everyone.
mistakes.fix: Right depends on whether the person faces the centre or outward.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting to use every clue.
mistakes.fix: Check that each clue is satisfied before choosing an answer.

memoryTip: Fix the frame, place definite seats, then fill relative gaps. For circles, fix one person and confirm facing.
