title: Linear rows of three to five people
objective: Fix positions in small linear rows using positional statements and produce the full order.
explanation: In linear seating, statements pin people to edges or relative positions: 'immediately left of', 'extreme right', or 'between'. Convert each clue into one or two fixed seats on a drawn strip. For someone facing you, their left is your right, so note the facing direction before translating left and right. Work from the most fixed clue (edges and middles) outward, then place flexible people last.
analogy: A row of seats is a film strip: each clue is one still frame; anchoring the clearest frame first lets every other frame snap into place beside it.

workedExamples.title: Three in a row
workedExamples.problem: A, B and C sit in a row. C is not at an extreme end. A is to the left of C. Who sits at the right end?
steps: Three seats: 1, 2, 3; C is at seat 2.
A is left of C, so A is at seat 1.
workedExamples.answer: B sits at the right end.

workedExamples.title: Four seats from three clues
workedExamples.problem: D, A, C, B and E sit in a row of five. C is in the middle. A is immediately left of C. D is at the extreme left. E is to the right of B. Find the order.
steps: C is seat 3; A is seat 2; D is seat 1.
Remaining seats 4 and 5 hold B and E.
E is right of B, so B = 4 and E = 5.
workedExamples.answer: The order is D, A, C, B, E.

rule.title: Anchor first
rule.detail: Fix extreme and middle positions before relative clues.

rule.title: Facing matters
rule.detail: A person facing you has their left on your right side.

rule.title: Fill leftovers
rule.detail: After anchors, remaining people fill the remaining seats with clues deciding ties.

rule.title: Verify all clues
rule.detail: Read every clue against the final order once before answering.

mistakes.mistake: Placing a relative clue before the anchor clue.
mistakes.fix: 'Immediately left of C' is useless until C's seat exists.

mistakes.mistake: Ignoring facing direction in circle or face-to-face rows.
mistakes.fix: For facing-center circles, right-hand side appears clockwise/left is anticlockwise; check conventions each time.

mistakes.mistake: Contradicting a clue with a leftover guess.
mistakes.fix: Re-check every clue; one violated clue invalidates the whole order.

memoryTip: Seats first for anchors, relations next, leftovers last, and a final clue-by-clue audit.

practice.prompt: Q is left of R and S is right of R in a 3-seat row. Who is in the middle?
practice.answer: R. Order is Q, R, S.

practice.prompt: Five people: P is 2nd from left; Q is at an end; P is left of Q. Is Q's end determinable?
practice.answer: No: Q can be at either end in the stated form unless more clues fix the others.

title: Five-seat deductions and facing-centre circles
objective: Solve five-to-six-person linear rows with negative clues and handle circular rows facing the centre with clockwise bookkeeping.
explanation: Harder rows include negative clues such as 'B is not adjacent to A' and 'not at an end'; these prune placements rather than pin them, so work seat by seat with the anchors first and prune afterwards. For circles facing the centre, the convention is: the left hand of a person faces the chair anticlockwise from theirs... standard usage places a person's right side on the chair that comes clockwise? No: facing the centre, rights run anticlockwise for the viewer; the safe habit is to pick one heading (right = anticlockwise) and hold it through the problem.
analogy: A circular table turned inside out is a clock face: once you fix one hand as clockwise, each clue is a fixed number of minute-steps between neighbours.

workedExamples.title: Linear five with negatives
workedExamples.problem: Five friends A, B, C, D, E in a row. A is immediately right of B. C is not adjacent to D. D is at the left end. E is between A and C. Determine the order.
steps: E lies between A and C, so A, E, C or C, E, A occupy three consecutive seats with E in the middle.
A must sit immediately right of B, so B, A is an adjacent pair.
Testing A, E, C on seats 2-4 gives no legal seat for B; move the triple right by one.
So A(3), E(4), C(5) and B sits immediately left of A at seat 2.

workedExamples.title: Circle facing centre
workedExamples.problem: P, Q, R sit in a circle facing the centre with P to the right of Q (right taken anticlockwise). If P faces a fixed reference, describe their clockwise order.
steps: P is one anticlockwise step from Q.
So clockwise the order is Q to P, with the third person R free in the remaining chair unless clues fix it.
State assumptions explicitly so the answer stays provable.
workedExamples.answer: Clockwise: Q, P, then R in the free seat.

rule.title: Negative clues prune
rule.detail: Use them after anchors to strike forbidden chairs.

rule.title: Between needs a facing
rule.detail: Only apply between-statements once left-right orientation is fixed.

rule.title: Circle convention
rule.detail: Pick right = anticlockwise for facing-centre circles and state it once.

rule.title: Full verification
rule.detail: Read all clues against the final arrangement; negative clues included.

mistakes.mistake: Applying 'not adjacent' before anchors exist.
mistakes.fix: Pruning needs a chosen seat grid first.

mistakes.mistake: Collapsing between-orientations too early.
mistakes.fix: Keep both possible orders until a clue rejects one.

mistakes.mistake: Mixing clockwise conventions mid-problem.
mistakes.fix: Fix the handedness at the start of the question and keep it.

memoryTip: Anchor, place pairs, prune negatives, choose one circle handedness; audit every clue at the end.

practice.prompt: Row of 4: P is 2nd from left, Q at an end, Q right of P. Which end has Q?
practice.answer: Right end. P seat 2, Q seat 4.

practice.prompt: Circle: faces centre, A right of B (anticlockwise reading). Give the clockwise order of two people.

title: Two facing rows and dual-key circles
objective: Coordinate two rows facing each other and resolve circular arrangements where each person knows both neighbours.
explanation: Two-row setups place a row facing another; clues may link partners across rows (opposite seats) or within rows, so keep two anchored seat maps side by side and mark cross-row pairs. In circles, adjacent-pair clues may be one-sided (A right of B) or double-sided (A adjacent to B); double-sided clues leave two distinct placements until a facing note resolves handedness. Negative clues prune forbidden chairs exactly as in linear solving.
analogy: Two facing rows are opposing bookshelves: each shelf is arranged alone, then clamped by the pairs you decide run across the aisle.

workedExamples.title: Row facing row
workedExamples.problem: Rows 1 (P, Q, R) and 2 (A, B, C) face each other. R is opposite A. P faces C? Let us use: R opposite A, Q opposite B, P opposite C; plus internal clue Q immediately right of P (viewed from row-1's own facing). Describe row 1's order.
steps: Cross pairs fix which column each row-1 person occupies, but internal order still needs the right-hand clue.
With Q immediately right of P, and R then completing the row, the row-1 order is P, Q, R.
Check: Q sits immediately right of P in their own facing.
workedExamples.answer: Row 1 reads P, Q, R from their left.

workedExamples.title: Circle with double clue
workedExamples.problem: Five friends around a circle facing the centre. A is adjacent to B, and B is adjacent to C. How many seats may A and C each occupy?
steps: Fix B anywhere (circle rotation is free).
A occupies either chair beside B; C likewise.
Without a handedness note, A and C each have 2 possible chairs; the remaining two seats stay for the other two friends.
workedExamples.answer: Each of A and C has 2 placements; total pairings 2 x 2 = 4 until one more clue resolves them.

rule.title: Two maps, one clamp
rule.detail: Arrange each row by its internal clues; cross-row pairs clamp the relative shift.

rule.title: One-sided vs double
rule.detail: 'Right of' fixes handedness; 'adjacent to' leaves two options until resolved.

rule.title: Rotation freedom
rule.detail: Circles have no absolute seat: fix one person as the anchor.

rule.title: Negative pruning
rule.detail: 'Not adjacent' strikes chairs after placements exist.

mistakes.mistake: Mixing the two rows' handedness conventions.
mistakes.fix: Each row faces the other; left for one row is the other's right side of the aisle.

mistakes.mistake: Treating adjacent clues as fixing order.
mistakes.fix: Adjacent means two mirror options until another clue breaks the tie.

mistakes.mistake: Anchoring circles to an absolute corner.
mistakes.fix: Only relative anchors exist around a circle.

memoryTip: Clamp cross-aisle pairs, keep facing conventions per row, anchor circles internally.

practice.prompt: Circle facing centre: A right of B (anticlockwise), B adjacent to C. How many C placements?
practice.answer: Two (either side of B), unless handedness locks further.

practice.prompt: Row facing row with fixed cross pairs; internal clue R between P and Q (linear order with 3). Row order?
practice.answer: Either P, R, Q or Q, R, P without a handedness note.

practice.prompt: Why can two facing rows disagree on left and right?
practice.answer: Each person's left is body-facing; facing opposite directions mirrors the axes.

title: Never-together counts and alternating circles
objective: Count seatings under no-adjacency constraints and alternating rings with fixed gender parity.
explanation: Constraint counting rejects illegal blocks: seating 5 people in a row where two specified people must never sit together counts total 5! minus the pair-fused arrangements 4! x 2 = 48, giving 120 - 48 = 72. For circles with alternating genders, fix the men's ring first as (4 - 1)! = 6 arrangements, then seat the 4 women in the 4 gaps in 4! = 24 ways, totalling 144.
analogy: Constraint counting is boarding a plane: total seatings minus the layouts that weld the feuding pair to one shoulder-turned block, and alternating rings are man-woman-man slots between each anchor.

workedExamples.title: Never together in a row
workedExamples.problem: In how many ways can 5 people sit in a row if A and B refuse to sit together?
steps: Fuse A and B into one block: 4 units in a row with 2 internal orders: 4! x 2 = 48.

workedExamples.title: Alternating circle
workedExamples.problem: Four men and four women sit around a round table, alternating genders. How many distinct seatings?
steps: Anchor the circle: men form a ring in (4 - 1)! = 6 arrangements.
Four gaps between men take the 4 women in 4! = 24 ways.

rule.title: Block subtraction
rule.detail: Never-together = total - fused-block arrangements.

rule.title: Round fixing
rule.detail: Fix one anchor to remove rotational repetition.

rule.title: Gap filling
rule.detail: Alternating circles place the second group into the first group's gaps.

rule.title: Order inside the block
rule.detail: Remember the fused pair's 2 internal orders before subtracting.

mistakes.mistake: Subtracting 24 (4!) instead of 48.
mistakes.fix: A fused block still allows AB or BA inside: multiply by 2 first.

mistakes.mistake: Using 4! for the men's circle.
mistakes.fix: Rotations collapse: (n - 1)!

mistakes.mistake: Doubling necklaces with gendered alternation.
mistakes.fix: Alternation is a constraint, not a reflection; only mirror-symmetric bead necklaces halve.

memoryTip: Total minus welded pairs; circles anchor at one seat; alternate rings fill gaps.

practice.answer: 24. Weld AB as a unit: 4 other units around circle: (5-1)! = 24 with internal order fixed.

title: Venn diagrams make syllogisms visible
objective: Test conclusions against every possible Venn arrangement of the given statements.
explanation: Translate 'All A are B' as A inside B, 'No A is B' as disjoint circles, and 'Some A are B' as an overlap. A conclusion follows only if it is true in every diagram consistent with the statements. Do not add real-world knowledge; use only the stated relationships.
analogy: Statements are constraints on a diagram. A conclusion is valid only if every legal drawing satisfies it, not just one convenient drawing.

workedExamples.title: All and some
workedExamples.problem: Statements: All roses are flowers. Some flowers are red. Does 'Some roses are red' follow?
steps: The red flowers may or may not overlap roses.
There is a valid diagram with no red rose.
workedExamples.answer: No, it does not necessarily follow.

workedExamples.title: Exclusion
workedExamples.problem: Statements: All roses are flowers. No flowers are stones. Does 'No roses are stones' follow?
steps: Flowers are completely separate from stones.
Therefore roses are separate from stones.

rule.title: All A are B
rule.detail: A is a subset of B.

rule.title: No A is B
rule.detail: A and B are disjoint.

rule.title: Some A are B
rule.detail: At least one element lies in both.

rule.title: Validity test
rule.detail: A conclusion follows only if it holds in every possible diagram.

rule.title: Complement
rule.detail: If all A are B and no B is C, then no A is C.

mistakes.mistake: Using real-world facts to fill gaps.
mistakes.fix: Use only the stated premises.

mistakes.mistake: Treating 'some' as 'some but not all'.
mistakes.fix: In logic, 'some' means at least one and may include all.

mistakes.mistake: Accepting a conclusion that is true in only one diagram.
mistakes.fix: Test a diagram where the overlap is absent or different.

memoryTip: All means inside, none means apart, some means overlap. A conclusion must survive every legal diagram.

title: Chain syllogisms in two lines
objective: Derive valid conclusions from two linked statements involving All and Some, and avoid the classic conversion traps.
explanation: A syllogism gives two statements and asks which conclusion must follow. All A are B is a chain arrow from A into B: linking two arrows through a shared middle term transfers from one end to the other, so All A are B and All B are C force All A are C. Some A are B is a two-way overlap, so it links forward and backward. A safe conversion rule: All A are B implies Some B are A, but the reverse and the symmetric reading are invalid.
analogy: Statements are roads: All is a one-way express lane, Some is a two-way street; a conclusion is valid only if you can drive it entirely on existing roads without paving new ones.

workedExamples.title: Two chains joined
workedExamples.problem: Statements: All pens are books. All books are red. Conclusion: All pens are red. Valid or invalid?
steps: Arrow 1 points pens into books; arrow 2 points books into red.
The middle term books connects the two chains.
The combined arrow runs pens into red.

workedExamples.title: Safe conversion
workedExamples.problem: Given: All cats are animals. Which single conclusion is certainly true?
steps: The valid conversion is Some animals are cats.
All animals are cats would reverse the arrow wrongly.
Some cats are not animals contradicts the statement.

rule.title: All is a one-way arrow
rule.detail: All A are B admits no arrow from B back to A except the weak Some B are A.

rule.title: Some is two-way
rule.detail: Some A are B equals Some B are A.

rule.title: Chain through the middle
rule.detail: Two All statements joined through a shared middle term give a direct All conclusion across the ends.

rule.title: No invention
rule.detail: A conclusion needs a full road of statements; missing roads make it a maybe, not a must.

mistakes.mistake: Converting All A are B into All B are A.
mistakes.fix: Only the weak Some B are A conversion is valid.

mistakes.mistake: Treating Some A are B as All A are B or as Some A are not B.
mistakes.fix: Some leaves room for all; it never asserts part-outside.

mistakes.mistake: Using a term that appears in no statement.
mistakes.fix: Every word in a valid conclusion appears in the statements.

memoryTip: All arrows pump one way, Some streets both ways, and conclusions only travel existing roads.

practice.prompt: All roses are flowers. All flowers fade. Does it follow that all roses fade?
practice.answer: Yes, by chaining the two All statements through flowers.

practice.prompt: No reptiles are birds. Is 'some reptiles are not birds' valid?
practice.answer: Yes; a full exclusion implies the weak positive split in the negative direction.

practice.prompt: All parrots are birds. Some birds fly. Can we conclude all parrots fly?
practice.answer: No; the flying birds may not include any parrots.

title: No-statements, some-not and full conclusion tables
objective: Draw valid inferences when No-statements and Some-not statements appear, and read full conclusion verdicts table-style.
explanation: No A are B is a wall between the sets; any conclusion crossing it is invalid, but the wall lets you assert No A are C when C lies on or beyond B's outside link. Some A are not B says at least one member of A avoids B, which can support Some-not conclusions downstream but supports nothing that needs overlap. A conversion table keeps this honest: All A are B converts to Some B are A; Some A are B converts to Some B are A; No A are B converts to No B are A; Some A are not B converts to nothing.
analogy: All is a pipe, Some is a shared window, No is a wall, and Some-not is a hole in the fence on one side only; conclusions must reuse exactly these structures in both directions they claim.

workedExamples.title: Wall transfer
workedExamples.problem: Statements: All A are B. No B are C. Conclusion: No A are C. Valid?
steps: B walls off C, so nothing inside B can be C.
A's members, being inside B, cannot be C.

workedExamples.title: Wall and window compose
workedExamples.problem: Statements: Some A are B. No A are C. Conclusion: Some B are not C. Valid?
steps: Some A are B guarantees at least one member of B that is also in A.
No A are C is a wall between A and C, so that very member cannot be C.
Hence at least one member of B lies outside C.
workedExamples.answer: Valid: some B are not C.

rule.title: Conversion table
rule.detail: All A-B to Some B-A; Some A-B to Some B-A; No A-B to No B-A; Some A-not-B to nothing.

rule.title: Wall chaining
rule.detail: Inside-of-All plus a No-wall transfers the wall inward across the contained set.

rule.title: Overlap needs overlap
rule.detail: Any Some conclusion downstream requires an overlapping statement to reach it.

rule.title: Draw the four cases
rule.detail: When unsure, sketch worst-case diagrams; one counter-case kills validity.

mistakes.mistake: Converting Some A are not B.
mistakes.fix: That sentence has no valid two-way conversion.

mistakes.mistake: Believing No statements imply Some-not conclusions automatically.
mistakes.fix: No A are B does not assert a non-empty A; Some-not statements need members.

mistakes.mistake: Chaining through a wall rather than against it.
mistakes.fix: Walls block crossing; chain on the contained side only.

memoryTip: Learn the four conversions; walls move inward through All sets; Some-not converts to nothing.

practice.prompt: All desks are chairs. No chairs are lamps. Valid conclusion?
Some keys are locks. Valid conversion?
Some pens are not pencils. Does 'no pencils are pens' follow?
practice.answer: No; the statements overlap partly; a No-conclusion is too strong.

title: Possibility boxes and three-conclusion verdicts
objective: Test possibility-based conclusions with diagram cases and deliver instance-by-instance verdicts on multi-conclusion sets.
explanation: Possibility questions ask whether a diagram can exist that satisfies all statements and the extra claim; the verdict is yes or no depending on whether the statements force the claim false. Their cousin, the multi-conclusion verdict, grades several candidate conclusions; each is checked against the statements with 'must follow' discipline, one counter-case killing it. Venn sketches with deliberate corner cases are the tool of record, and the conversion table remains the algebra of record.
analogy: Possibility questions are room-layout puzzles: statements are walls that must stand in every layout; a claim survives if at least one legal layout contains it.

workedExamples.title: Possibility layout
workedExamples.problem: Statements: All A are B. Some B are C. Is a layout possible where some C are A?
steps: Draw B as a large set; A strictly inside it.
Place part of C overlapping B; a sliver of C may also overlap the A region because C overlaps B.
This layout satisfies both statements and the claim.
workedExamples.answer: Yes, possible; the claim is not forced but it is not forbidden either.

workedExamples.title: Forced false claim
workedExamples.problem: Statements: All A are B. No B are C. Is any C being A possible?
steps: The wall No B are C excludes every C from B's interior.
So no member of C can lie in A.
workedExamples.answer: No; the statements force the claim false.

rule.title: Possibility = one legal layout
rule.detail: Build a layout satisfying both statements and the claim; failure means impossible.

rule.title: Must-follow verdicts
rule.detail: Each conclusion stands alone; one counter-case clears it to invalid.

rule.title: Walls dominate
rule.detail: No-statements forbid layouts; All-statements confine members.

rule.title: Conversion table still applies
rule.detail: Use the table's four conversions before diagramming.

mistakes.mistake: Calling unforced conclusions invalid in possibility questions.
mistakes.fix: Possibility asks can, not must; unforced means possible.

mistakes.mistake: Drafting layouts that violate a No-statement.
mistakes.fix: Walls stand in every layout; resketch around them.

mistakes.mistake: Grading conclusions against each other instead of the statements.
mistakes.fix: Each verdict cites the statements only.

memoryTip: Possibility wants one legal sketch; verdicts want zero legal counterexamples; walls always stand.

practice.prompt: All cats are animals; some animals are pets. Is 'some pets are cats' possible?
practice.answer: Yes; draw pets overlapping the cat region inside animals.

practice.prompt: All pens are items; no items are liquids. Possible that some liquid is a pen?

practice.answer: Yes; chain the two overlaps through locks.

title: Three-verdict drill on chained statements
objective: Deliver must-follow verdicts on a set of three candidate conclusions against chained statements.
explanation: Given: All A are B and No B are C. Three verdicts: (1) No A are C - valid, since A sits wholly inside B and the wall blocks all of B from C. (2) Some C are not A - valid, because C lies fully outside B, hence outside A, and C is taken non-empty by diagram convention. (3) All C are A - invalid, contradicting the wall. Each verdict stands on the statements alone, with one counter-example enough to fail.
analogy: A verdict exercise is a referee reviewing three goals: each stands or falls on the field's own lines, never on the crowd's expectations.

workedExamples.title: Verdict one and two
workedExamples.problem: Statements: All A are B. No B are C. Verdict on: (1) No A are C; (2) Some C are not A.
steps: (1) A is inside B; B is walled from C; so nothing of A is C: valid.
(2) C lies entirely outside B and hence outside A; C is non-empty, so at least one C avoids A: valid.

workedExamples.title: Verdict three
workedExamples.problem: Same statements; verdict on: (3) All C are A.
steps: C is outside B while A is inside B.
Any member of C would violate the wall if it were also A.

rule.title: One counterexample kills
rule.detail: A conclusion unsatisfied by one legal diagram is invalid.

rule.title: Walls dominate
rule.detail: No-statements forbid overlap regardless of other claims.

rule.title: Non-empty convention
rule.detail: Exam diagrams treat named sets as existing, licensing some-conclusions over disjoint sets.

rule.title: Cite the statements
rule.detail: Every verdict quotes the two statements, never the other candidates.

mistakes.mistake: Marking (2) invalid because C and A were never mentioned together.
mistakes.fix: Transitivity through the wall B gives C's full separation from A; the some-verdict then follows.

mistakes.mistake: Letting one verdict influence another.
mistakes.fix: Each conclusion is judged in isolation.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting the non-empty diagram convention.
mistakes.fix: Some-certainties rely on the set being drawn with at least one member.

memoryTip: Judge verdicts solo; walls and containment carry them; disjoint non-empty sets license some claims.

practice.answer: Valid: statues are disjoint from animals, hence from cats.

title: Conclusions must be forced by the statement
objective: Separate what a statement guarantees from what is merely plausible, and judge assumptions and arguments carefully.
explanation: A conclusion follows only when it must be true given the statement. An assumption is an unstated premise the argument depends on. A strong argument is directly relevant, material and logically connected to the statement. Avoid bringing in extra facts or treating a possibility as a certainty.
analogy: A statement is a locked box of facts. A conclusion is valid only if it is already inside the box, not if it might fit nearby.

workedExamples.title: Conditional warning
workedExamples.problem: Statement: 'The company will close the factory if losses continue.' Conclusions: I. Losses are continuing. II. The factory has closed. Do either follow?
steps: The statement is conditional: closure happens only if losses continue.
It does not say losses are continuing.
It does not say closure has happened.

workedExamples.title: Strong argument
workedExamples.problem: Statement: 'A city should improve public transport.' Argument: 'It can reduce traffic congestion and commute time.' Is the argument strong?
steps: The argument is directly relevant to public transport.
It gives a concrete benefit connected to the proposal.
It does not rely on an unrelated personal preference.

rule.title: Must versus may
rule.detail: A valid conclusion must be true, not merely possible.

rule.title: Conditional logic
rule.detail: 'If P then Q' does not prove P or Q by itself.

rule.title: Assumption
rule.detail: Ask what unstated belief the argument needs in order to work.

rule.title: Strong argument
rule.detail: Relevant, material and logically linked to the proposal.

mistakes.mistake: Converting 'if' into 'therefore'.
mistakes.fix: Keep the conditional direction; do not affirm the antecedent or consequent automatically.

mistakes.mistake: Rejecting a conclusion because it seems unlikely in real life.
mistakes.fix: Judge only logical necessity from the statement.

mistakes.mistake: Calling an irrelevant emotional appeal a strong argument.
mistakes.fix: Check direct relevance and material impact.

memoryTip: Ask: does the statement force this? If it only permits it, the conclusion does not follow.

practice.prompt: Statement: 'All employees completed training.' Does 'Some employees completed training' follow?
practice.answer: Yes; if all did, then at least one did, provided the group is non-empty.

practice.prompt: Statement: 'If it rains, the match is cancelled.' It is not raining. Is the match necessarily played?
practice.answer: No; the statement specifies only what happens if it rains.

practice.prompt: What makes an argument strong?
practice.answer: Direct relevance, material evidence and a logical connection to the claim.

title: What must follow and what merely sounds likely
objective: Decide whether a suggested conclusion is logically forced by a statement or merely plausible.
explanation: A conclusion is valid only when the statement's words force it; plausibility, humour or statistics from outside the statement cannot rescue it. Words like only, all, none and at least carry the logical load, so read them precisely. Advice, examples and opinions inside a statement are not facts themselves. If any reasonable situation satisfies the statement but breaks the conclusion, the conclusion is invalid.
analogy: The statement is a contract; a conclusion is valid only inside the exact wording of the contract, never on what an honest person would probably assume.

workedExamples.title: A forced superlative
workedExamples.problem: Statement: The city recorded its lowest temperature in ten years. Conclusion: The temperature in each of the previous nine years was higher. Valid or invalid?
steps: Lowest in ten years means every other year in the window was warmer.
So the stated comparison forces each earlier year to be higher.

workedExamples.title: A likely but unforced link
workedExamples.problem: Statement: The government increased the tax on rice. Conclusion: Every household's rice bill will increase. Valid or invalid?
steps: Tax increase does not force retail bill increase; subsidies, stock or diet changes may absorb it.
A single contrary scenario suffices to invalidate.
The conclusion needs weaker wording like may increase to be acceptable.

rule.title: Forced, not likely
rule.detail: Validity needs necessity; probable is a fail.

rule.title: Weight-bearing words
rule.detail: Only, all, none, at least and superlatives decide answers; read them slowly.

rule.title: No outside stats
rule.detail: General knowledge exceptions may not override the statement, but missing logical links invalidate it.

rule.title: Contrary scenario test
rule.detail: If one sensible scenario fits the statement yet breaks the conclusion, conclude invalid.

mistakes.mistake: Marking emotionally convincing lines as valid.
mistakes.fix: Re-read for necessity, not persuasiveness.

mistakes.mistake: Treating an example inside the statement as a universal rule.
mistakes.fix: One case described in a statement does not cover all cases.

mistakes.mistake: Skipping the wording of the conclusion itself.
mistakes.fix: Conclusion wording may overstate the statement by one word; check each term.

memoryTip: Necessity over plausibility; superlatives and only-words are the hinges; one contrary scenario sinks a conclusion.

practice.prompt: Statement: All employees must wear badges inside the plant. Conclusion: Badges are required somewhere in the plant. Valid?
practice.answer: Yes; inside the plant is a location with a requirement.

practice.prompt: Statement: Sales doubled this quarter. Conclusion: Sales last quarter were zero. Valid?
practice.answer: No; doubling twice a positive number is possible, so zero is not forced.

practice.prompt: Statement: The notice was read aloud for all to hear. Conclusion: Some people heard the notice. Valid?
practice.answer: Yes; read aloud for all to hear forces an audience.

title: Courses of action and argument strength
objective: Rate suggested courses of action as practical follow-ups and grade arguments as strong or weak against a stated situation.
explanation: Two exam variants extend plain conclusions. Courses of action ask whether a proposal is a reasonable step given the statement: strong follow-ups act directly on the stated cause, are practical, and do not contradict the problem; follow-ups that leap beyond it, repeat the problem or promise impossible outcomes are weak. Argument questions grade claims as strong or weak: strong arguments tie to the stated fact, are widely-workable points of practical wisdom, and address the main issue; weak ones are generalities, anecdotes or tangents.
analogy: Courses of action are fire-safety drills: a strong drill attacks the specific fire reported; a drill for a different fire, or one pointing everywhere, fails the building.

workedExamples.title: Course of action grading
workedExamples.problem: Statement: Frequent power cuts hit the industrial area. Course: The state should set up an additional power plant in that region. Strong or weak?
steps: The course addresses the stated cause directly (shortfall of supply).
It is practical and within normal policy steps.
It does not contradict the problem.

workedExamples.title: Weak-argument pattern
workedExamples.problem: Statement: City buses remain overcrowded. Argument: Buses are public property, so overcrowding should be tolerated. Strong or weak?
steps: The argument does not address the problem itself.
It uses ownership as if it forced tolerance, which is a generality.
Service logic, not ownership, would be the main issue.

rule.title: Direct action wins
rule.detail: A course of action that acts on the stated cause and is feasible is strong.

rule.title: Nothing-too-far
rule.detail: Courses beyond the statement's scope, or stemming from unmentioned politics, are weak.

rule.title: Argument checklist
rule.detail: Relevance, practical wisdom, and main-issue focus define strength.

rule.title: Experience-based claims
rule.detail: Widely-accepted administrative or economic wisdom counts; single anecdotes do not.

mistakes.mistake: Rating ambitious plans strong by intention alone.
mistakes.fix: Feasibility within the statement is required.

mistakes.mistake: Dismissing generic wisdom as weak in every case.
mistakes.fix: Common administrative wisdom applied correctly is strong; it fails only when tangential.

mistakes.mistake: Picking arguments that restate the problem with a complaint.
mistakes.fix: A complaint is not an argument until it proposes workable reasoning.

memoryTip: Direct, feasible, on-issue means strong; scope-external or generic means weak.

practice.prompt: Statement: Airport congestion rising. Course: Add screening staff at peak hours. Strong or weak?
practice.answer: Strong; direct and feasible on the stated cause.

practice.prompt: Statement: River polluted upstream. Course: Ban all boats on the whole river. Strong or weak?
practice.answer: Weak; overbroad beyond the stated cause region.

practice.prompt: Argument: Plants must be watered, so offices should water theirs. Strong or weak for an office-greening case?
practice.answer: Strong if the case concerns plant upkeep; weak if the case is about air quality instead.

title: Hidden assumptions and advertisement logic
objective: Surface the implicit assumptions inside persuasive statements and grade promotional claims against stated facts.
explanation: Assumption questions read under the statement's floor: every persuasive line relies on unstated premises, such as a notice assuming people read notices, or a product campaign assuming its advertised feature matters to buyers. Valid assumptions are necessary for the statement to work and stay within its world; they must not be stronger than the statement. Advertisement logic adds effect claims, whose assessment checks whether the claimed effect follows from the stated mechanism at all.
analogy: Assumptions are floor joists: invisible but load-bearing; your job is to tap each joist and decide whether the statement would collapse without it.

workedExamples.title: Notice assumption
workedExamples.problem: Statement: Please switch off lights when leaving. An implicit assumption?
steps: The notice is worth issuing only if someone reads it.
More precisely: people leaving the room will comply if asked.
Both are necessary for the request to function.
workedExamples.answer: People read and follow such notices.

workedExamples.title: Over-strong assumption
workedExamples.problem: Statement: Our new mixer uses less electricity. Candidate assumption: no other mixer brand sells in the market. Valid?
steps: The statement functions without any claim about market structure.
The candidate assumption is neither necessary nor tied to the claim.
An honest necessary premise: buyers care about electricity use.

rule.title: Necessary, not sufficient
rule.detail: Assumptions must be required for the statement to make sense, not merely helpful.

rule.title: Stay inside the world
rule.detail: Market-wide or universal claims exceed a local statement's needs.

rule.title: Effect follows mechanism
rule.detail: Promotional effect claims need a stated mechanism that plausibly produces the effect.

rule.title: Negation test
rule.detail: Negate the candidate assumption; if the statement collapses, it is necessary.

mistakes.mistake: Listing helpful extras as assumptions.
mistakes.fix: Apply the negation test; helpful-without-necessary fails.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming universal follow-through ('everyone will comply').
mistakes.fix: Assumptions stay proportionate: enough compliance for the statement to matter.

mistakes.mistake: Grading persuasive tone instead of logical necessity.
mistakes.fix: Structure beats style in these questions.

memoryTip: Joists tap test: necessary or nothing; proportionate strength; mechanisms must connect to effects.

practice.prompt: Statement: Buy two, get one free. Necessary assumption?
practice.answer: Customers respond to the offer, i.e. buyers exist and notice it.

practice.prompt: Statement: The train will arrive on time. Assumption: weather will stay clear. Necessary?
practice.answer: Yes when the statement's reliability depends on conditions; treated as necessary in exam conventions.

practice.prompt: Candidate assumption: 'No one ever switches off lights.' Valid for the switch-off notice?
practice.answer: No; it contradicts the notice's very premise of possible compliance.

title: Assumption drills with the negation test
objective: Grade candidate assumptions by necessity and proportion, applying the negation test.
explanation: An assumption must be necessary: if negating it collapses the statement's point, it stays; if the statement survives without it, the candidate is merely helpful and fails. Proportion matters too: an assumption claiming everyone will comply outruns a notice's needs - enough compliance will do. A study-method notice, for example, assumes both that students read notices and that they can adopt the method, but not that they will succeed.
analogy: Assumptions are load-bearing joists: tap each candidate with the negation hammer - survivors are joists, ones the house never needed are decoration.

workedExamples.title: Negation test pass
workedExamples.problem: Statement: Students should try the new revision method for best results. Candidate assumption: notices like this reach the students they concern. Valid?
steps: Negate: notices never reach the relevant students.
The advice loses its audience and point.
So the assumption is necessary: valid.

workedExamples.title: Outrunning the statement
workedExamples.problem: Same statement; candidate assumption: every student who tries the method will succeed. Valid?
steps: The statement promises best results only if tried, not guaranteed success.
Universal success is a stronger claim than needed.

rule.title: Negation test
rule.detail: Negating a true assumption frustrates the statement; negating a false one changes nothing.

rule.title: Proportionality
rule.detail: Assumptions claim no more than the statement needs: many, not all.

rule.title: Inside the world
rule.detail: Assumptions live among people, habits and feasible acts named or implied by the statement.

rule.title: Success vs opportunity
rule.detail: Notices assume opportunity, not guaranteed outcomes.

mistakes.mistake: Failing necessary-but-implicit joists because they sound obvious.
mistakes.fix: Obvious and necessary are different axes; the test decides.

mistakes.mistake: Accepting universal claims as assumptions.
mistakes.fix: Everyone will comply overreaches; use enough-scope wording.

mistakes.mistake: Testing tone instead of necessity.
mistakes.fix: Run the negation hammer, not the style checker.

memoryTip: Tap with the negation hammer: necessary survives, decoration falls.

practice.answer: Valid: without readers the notice has no effect.

practice.prompt: Statement: Attendance is mandatory. Assumption: attendance is recorded?
practice.answer: Not necessary for the instruction's validity: mandatary rules can exist un-enforced; helpful but not required.

practice.prompt: Statement: Try method A; it works. Assumption: users can follow method A's steps?
practice.answer: Valid: an unusable method's recommendation collapses.

title: Name the relationship before choosing
objective: Identify the precise relationship in a word, number or symbol analogy and apply the same relationship.
explanation: State the link in a short sentence: 'A doctor works in a hospital' or '8 is the cube of 2'. Then test the options against that same sentence. Watch for relationships that can be read in more than one direction. For number analogies, check operations, squares, cubes, primes and digit patterns.

workedExamples.problem: Doctor : Hospital :: Teacher : ?
steps: A doctor works in a hospital.
A teacher works in a school.
Choose the option that names the workplace.

rule.title: State the relation
rule.detail: Write a precise sentence connecting the first pair before looking at options.

rule.title: Same direction
rule.detail: Preserve the order of the relationship: cause-effect and part-whole are not reversible.

rule.title: Number checks
rule.detail: Test addition, multiplication, squares, cubes and digit reversals.

rule.title: Eliminate
rule.detail: Reject options that fit a different or weaker relationship.

mistakes.mistake: Choosing an option that is merely associated with the word.
mistakes.fix: Match the exact relationship, not a loose topic connection.

mistakes.mistake: Reversing a cause-effect relation.
mistakes.fix: Keep the first pair in the same order as the question.

mistakes.mistake: Stopping at the first number pattern that seems to fit.

title: Match the relationship, not the topic
objective: Identify the exact relationship in a word pair and select the option pair that mirrors it.
explanation: An analogy a : b :: c : ? succeeds only when the relation between c and the answer mirrors the relation between a and b, not when the two pairs merely share a topic. First name the relationship in one short phrase such as young one of, worker to workplace, part to whole, opposite, or a number rule like square or cube. Then test each option against the same named rule. Number analogies encode arithmetic: 8 : 64 is a square, 5 : 125 a cube.
analogy: Word analogies are dances: pick out the step (young-one, opposite, square) and find the pair performing the same step, however different the music.

workedExamples.title: Young one relation
workedExamples.problem: Cat : Kitten :: Dog : ?  Options: hound, puppy, kennel, bark.

Test: the young one of a dog is a puppy.
Hound is an adult type, kennel is a place, bark is a sound.

rule.title: Name the relation
rule.detail: State the exact link in one short phrase before checking options.

rule.title: Same dance, new stage
rule.detail: The answer pair need not share the topic of the question pair, only the relation.

rule.title: Number rules
rule.detail: Check square, cube, double, half and prime relations in number analogies.

rule.title: Reverse trap
rule.detail: An option that answers b : a rather than a : b is wrong.

mistakes.fix: Animal pairs fail when the relation is young-one; hound is an animal but not a kitten analogue.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming arithmetic relations without testing.
mistakes.fix: Try squares, cubes, multiples of a fixed factor and digit sums in order.

mistakes.mistake: Missing direction of comparison.
mistakes.fix: Worker : Tool is not Tool : Worker; preserve order.

memoryTip: Name the step, mirror the step; for numbers try square, cube, double, and digit tricks in that order.

title: Letter and number-position analogies
objective: Solve alphabet-position analogies with shift or mirror rules and number analogies with mixed arithmetic relations.
explanation: Letter analogies break into positions: ABC to XYZ is a shift of 23 on each letter; ABC to ZYX is a full mirror (position p maps to 27 - p). Number analogies hide one operation: 26 is double 13 - then 13 relates to 65 how? Careful work at this level contains mixed two-operation relations such as multiply then add a constant; the strategy is to test single operations first, then pairs, and always verify the rule on the second member pair before choosing an option.
analogy: Letter analogies are slide rules and mirrors in the A1Z26 number line; number analogies are tiny machines whose gears you reverse-engineer from the two given pairs.

workedExamples.title: Shift analogy on letters
workedExamples.problem: Complete: ABC : DEF :: GHI : ?
steps: A to D is +3; B to E is +3; C to F is +3.
Apply +3 to G, H, I: J, K, L.

workedExamples.title: Two-step number rule
workedExamples.problem: Complete: 4 : 18 :: 7 : ? with relation multiply then add 2.
steps: Verify second pair wording: rule is x 4 + 2 exactly.

rule.title: Position shifts
rule.detail: Convert letters to numbers and test constant shifts first.

rule.title: Mirror mapping
rule.detail: p maps to 27 - p; palindromic pairs around M and N centre it.

rule.title: Operation pairs
rule.detail: If a single operation fails, test multiply-then-add and add-then-multiply patterns.

rule.title: Second-pair discipline
rule.detail: Verify the guessed rule reproduces the second given pair exactly.

mistakes.mistake: Shifting letters without converting to numbers.
mistakes.fix: Work on positions; E (5) plus 3 is H (8), not any near letter.

mistakes.mistake: Stopping at a close-but-wrong arithmetic fit.
mistakes.fix: Verify the rule on the second pair before matching options.

mistakes.mistake: Ignoring pairs that straddle Z or wrap around the alphabet.
mistakes.fix: Shifts on letters near Z may wrap; a stated rule decides wrapping.

memoryTip: Letters become numbers; shift, mirror or two-step gears; confirm the rule on the second pair.

title: Dual-relation and transformed-pair analogies
objective: Handle analogies whose relation is layered with two simultaneous rules and alphabet transforms such as mirror mappings and shifts.
explanation: Advanced analogies layer two relations at once: worker-to-place plus tool, or category-plus-quantity, so the winning option must satisfy both layers. Letter transforms stack too: a pair may be mirrored through 27 - position, shifted by a constant, or combinations of both, so tests must apply the calibrated rule exactly and verify it on the second pair. Number analogies may chain operations across a ratio with different operations per slot; verification on both member pairs is the standing discipline.
analogy: Advanced analogy pairs are duets: two instruments at once; the answer must play both parts, not merely echo the melody.

workedExamples.problem: Complete: Author : Novel :: Composer : ? with relation creator to major work.

workedExamples.problem: Complete: ABC : ZYX :: DEF : ?

Apply to DEF: D 4 maps to 23 = W, E 5 maps to 22 = V, F 6 maps to 21 = U.

rule.title: Both layers bind
rule.detail: An option satisfying one layer only is wrong.

rule.title: Stack order
rule.detail: Apply the transform functions in the calibrated order; test on the second member pair.

rule.title: Mirror arithmetic
rule.detail: 27 - position maps the alphabet inside out: A to Z, M to N; stack it with shifts when the example shows both.

rule.title: Slot-chained numbers
rule.detail: Each number pair may carry its own operation; read pairs as slots before generalising.

mistakes.mistake: Accepting topic-matching answers that miss one layer.
mistakes.fix: Score options layer by layer.

mistakes.mistake: Reordering transform steps inconsistently between pairs.
mistakes.fix: Calibrate once and reuse exactly.

mistakes.mistake: Extending a slot-specific number rule across all pairs.
mistakes.fix: Confirm the rule is global, or state the per-slot table.

title: Agreement, tense and clean sentences
objective: Spot subject-verb agreement, tense consistency and misplaced-modifier errors in placement tests.
explanation: A singular subject takes a singular verb; a plural subject takes a plural verb. In 'each', 'every', 'either' and 'neither' constructions, the subject is usually singular. Neither/nor verbs agree with the nearer subject. Keep tense consistent with the time marker. A modifier should sit next to the word it describes.
analogy: Grammar is traffic control: subjects and verbs must agree on the lane, tenses must stay in the same time zone, and modifiers must park next to the word they modify.

workedExamples.problem: Choose the correct verb: 'Each of the students ___ submitted the assignment.'
steps: The subject is 'each', which is singular.
The phrase 'of the students' does not change the subject.
workedExamples.answer: Each of the students has submitted the assignment.

workedExamples.title: Since with present perfect continuous
workedExamples.problem: Correct the sentence: 'He is working here since 2020.'
steps: 'Since 2020' marks a period continuing to the present.
Use present perfect continuous: has been working.
The completed sentence is 'He has been working here since 2020.'
workedExamples.answer: He has been working here since 2020.

rule.title: Subject-verb agreement
rule.detail: Match the verb to the actual subject, not to a noun in a prepositional phrase.

rule.title: Indefinite pronouns
rule.detail: Each, every, either and neither are singular in standard usage.

rule.title: Neither...nor
rule.detail: The verb agrees with the subject nearer to it.

rule.title: Time markers
rule.detail: Since/for with an action continuing now usually needs perfect or perfect continuous tense.

rule.title: Modifier placement
rule.detail: Place a describing phrase next to the noun it describes.

mistakes.mistake: Matching the verb to the nearest noun in a phrase.
mistakes.fix: Find the true subject first.

mistakes.mistake: Mixing past and present without a time shift.
mistakes.fix: Keep one time frame unless the meaning requires a change.

mistakes.mistake: Putting a modifier at the end so it describes the wrong noun.
mistakes.fix: Move it beside the intended noun.

memoryTip: Find the subject, ignore the phrase, match the verb. Time words choose the tense; modifiers sit beside their noun.

title: Subject-verb agreement
objective: Match verbs to singular and plural subjects, apply agreement with each, neither, either-or constructions and common collective nouns.
explanation: A verb agrees with its subject in number: singular subjects take the base verb with -s in the present (he goes), and plural subjects take the bare form (they go). Indefinite pronouns each, everyone, either and neither are singular even when followed by plural nouns. With either...or or neither...nor, the verb agrees with the nearest subject, and words named as school subjects or games, like mathematics or news, are singular.
analogy: Agreement is a handshake: the subject offers a hand of a certain size, and the verb must offer the matching hand, however crowded the sentence between them is.

The present form adds -s or -es: goes.

workedExamples.title: Neither is singular
workedExamples.problem: Choose the correct verb: Neither of the answers is / are correct.

rule.title: Singular s
rule.detail: Present tense third-person singular adds -s: goes, plays, watches.

rule.title: Indefinites are singular
rule.detail: Each, every, everyone, anyone, either, neither take singular verbs.

rule.title: Or-nor nearest
rule.detail: With either...or and neither...nor the verb follows the nearer subject.

rule.title: Looks plural, sounds singular

mistakes.mistake: Using a plural verb after each or neither.

title: Tense consistency and modal usage

title: Boolean values, constants and the three operators
objective: Model on/off logic with Boolean variables and constants, and evaluate AND, OR and NOT without second-guessing.
explanation: Boolean algebra is the algebra of two values. A Boolean variable can only be 0 or 1 (equivalently False or True), and a Boolean constant is one of those two values written directly in an expression. Three operators form the entire algebra: AND outputs 1 only when every input is 1; OR outputs 1 when at least one input is 1; NOT flips its single input from 0 to 1 or from 1 to 0. Every other idea in this topic — truth tables, identities, De Morgan's laws, simplification and logic gates — is built by combining these three operators, so being fast and certain with them is the foundation the rest of the chapter stands on.
analogy: Think of a light controlled by switches in series or parallel. Series switches (AND) need every switch on for the lamp to glow. Parallel switches (OR) light the lamp if any one path is closed. The NOT operator is simply swapping on for off on the same switch.

workedExamples.title: Reading an AND chain
workedExamples.problem: Evaluate A AND B AND C when A = 1, B = 0 and C = 1.
steps: AND requires every operand to be 1 for a result of 1.
The value of A and C cannot rescue the chain.
workedExamples.answer: 0, because a single 0 in an AND chain forces the whole chain to 0.

workedExamples.title: Reading an OR chain
workedExamples.problem: Evaluate A OR B OR C when A = 0, B = 1 and C = 0.
steps: OR requires at least one operand to be 1.
No need to check further operands.
workedExamples.answer: 1, because a single 1 in an OR chain forces the whole chain to 1.

workedExamples.title: Double negation
workedExamples.problem: Evaluate NOT (NOT A) when A = 0.
workedExamples.answer: 0 — NOT twice returns the original value (double negation law).

rule.title: AND is strict
rule.detail: A AND B = 1 only when A = 1 and B = 1; any 0 input makes the result 0. Identity: A AND 1 = A; A AND 0 = 0.

rule.title: OR is lenient
rule.detail: A OR B = 1 whenever at least one operand is 1. Identity: A OR 1 = 1; A OR 0 = A.

rule.title: NOT is a switch
rule.detail: NOT 0 = 1 and NOT 1 = 0. Applied twice it cancels: NOT (NOT A) = A.

rule.title: Constants beat variables
rule.detail: When a subexpression collapses to 0 or 1, substitute it immediately and simplify the rest of the expression first.

mistakes.mistake: Treating AND like OR or the reverse.
mistakes.fix: Remember the strictness order: AND needs all inputs = 1, OR needs any input = 1.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting that NOT applies to the whole expression after it, not just the next symbol.
mistakes.fix: Use parentheses explicitly: NOT (A OR B) is very different from (NOT A) OR B.

mistakes.mistake: Confusing Boolean 1/0 with numeric arithmetic.
mistakes.fix: There is no carry or borrowing: 1 + 1 OR-style means 1 OR 1 = 1, not decimal 2.

memoryTip: AND is the pessimist (all or nothing), OR is the optimist (any will do), NOT is the contrarian (always the opposite).

title: Truth tables and evaluating Boolean expressions
objective: Build complete truth tables for any Boolean expression and evaluate expressions with mixed AND, OR, NOT and XOR inputs.
explanation: A truth table is the complete catalogue of an expression: one row for every possible assignment of inputs, listing the output under that assignment. An expression with n variables has 2 to the power n rows, so three variables need eight rows. The reliable method is to evaluate the expression row by row: first replace the variables with the row's inputs, then apply NOT, then AND, then OR (with parentheses overriding that order). Placement tests frequently mix in XOR — the 'differences detector' that outputs 1 when its inputs disagree — so treat XOR as a fourth operator you can also expand: A XOR B equals (A AND NOT B) OR (NOT A AND B).
analogy: A truth table is like testing every possible key combination on a two-switch combination lock and recording whether the lock opens. You try each combination exactly once, and the table proves you covered them all.

workedExamples.title: Truth table for A OR (NOT A)
workedExamples.problem: Complete the truth table for the expression A OR (NOT A).
steps: Row A = 0: NOT A = 1, so 0 OR 1 = 1.
Row A = 1: NOT A = 0, so 1 OR 0 = 1.
workedExamples.answer: The output is 1 in every row — the expression is a tautology (the identity A OR (NOT A) = 1).

workedExamples.title: XOR of equals
workedExamples.problem: Evaluate A XOR B when A = 1 and B = 1, then when A = 1 and B = 0.
steps: XOR outputs 1 when the inputs differ.
1 and 1 do not differ, so the first result is 0.
1 and 0 differ, so the second result is 1.
workedExamples.answer: 0 for equal inputs, 1 for different inputs.

rule.title: Row count
rule.detail: An expression over n variables needs exactly 2^n rows — 2 for one variable, 4 for two, 8 for three.

rule.title: Evaluation order
rule.detail: Parentheses first, then NOT, then AND, then OR. When in doubt, add parentheses instead of trusting convention.

rule.title: XOR identity
rule.detail: A XOR B = (A AND NOT B) OR (NOT A AND B); alternatively A XOR B = 1 exactly when A and B differ.

rule.title: Tautology check
rule.detail: If every row of the truth table is 1 the two sides are logically equivalent — this is how laws such as De Morgan's are verified.

mistakes.mistake: Producing too few rows (for example 4 rows for three variables).
mistakes.fix: Count 2^n first and number the rows in binary order so no combination is missed.

mistakes.mistake: Evaluating NOT after AND/OR.
mistakes.fix: NOT always binds first (inside parentheses or over its own operand).

mistakes.mistake: Treating XOR as the same as OR.
mistakes.fix: XOR is 0 when both inputs are 1; plain OR would be 1 there.

memoryTip: Rows = 2^n. Evaluate like arithmetic: bracket, NOT, AND, OR. XOR just answers 'do these differ?'.

title: Laws, De Morgan and logic-gate simplification
objective: Use the Boolean laws and De Morgan's laws to simplify expressions, and map every simplified form onto its logic gates.
explanation: Boolean expressions simplify using a small lawbook. Absorption: A OR (A AND B) = A and A AND (A OR B) = A. Complement: A AND (NOT A) = 0 and A OR (NOT A) = 1. Distribution works like arithmetic: A AND (B OR C) = (A AND B) OR (A AND C), and also A OR (B AND C) = (A OR B) AND (A OR C). De Morgan's laws convert between AND and OR under negation: NOT (A AND B) = (NOT A) OR (NOT B), and NOT (A OR B) = (NOT A) AND (NOT B). Simplification matters because each operator in an expression corresponds to a gate in hardware — NOT maps to an inverter, AND/OR to their named gates, NAND/NOR to inverted outputs, XOR to a difference detector — and fewer operators mean fewer gates, less delay and lower cost. The standard exam technique is: expand with De Morgan, apply identities, then re-check with a truth table.
analogy: Simplifying a Boolean expression is like tidying a messy set of travel routes: De Morgan lets you re-route a forbiddance into permissions, absorption removes the detour that was already covered by a shorter road, and the truth table toll-checks that every destination is still reachable exactly as before.

Cancel the double negation: NOT (NOT B) = B.

workedExamples.problem: Simplify A OR (A AND B).
steps: If A = 1, the expression is 1 OR (1 AND B) = 1.
If A = 0, the expression is 0 OR (0 AND B) = 0.

workedExamples.title: Simplify then verify
workedExamples.problem: Simplify (A AND B) OR (NOT A AND B).
steps: Factor B: B AND (A OR NOT A).
Complement law: A OR NOT A = 1.
workedExamples.answer: B — a three-gate circuit collapses to a single wire.

rule.title: De Morgan's laws
rule.detail: NOT (A AND B) = (NOT A) OR (NOT B) — the AND becomes OR. NOT (A OR B) = (NOT A) AND (NOT B) — the OR becomes AND.

rule.title: Absorption laws
rule.detail: A OR (A AND B) = A; A AND (A OR B) = A.

rule.title: Complement laws
rule.detail: A AND (NOT A) = 0; A OR (NOT A) = 1; NOT (NOT A) = A.

rule.title: Gate mapping
rule.detail: NOT -> inverter; AND/OR -> their gates; NAND/NOR -> the universal gates that alone can build any circuit; XOR -> 1 when inputs differ.

mistakes.mistake: Applying De Morgan without flipping the operator.
mistakes.fix: The negation must move through the bracket AND change AND into OR (or OR into AND).

mistakes.mistake: Simplifying without re-checking equivalence.
mistakes.fix: Produce the truth table of the original and the simplified expression; they must match on every row.

mistakes.mistake: Distributing AND and OR as if only AND distributes.
mistakes.fix: In Boolean algebra both distribute: A OR (B AND C) = (A OR B) AND (A OR C), unlike ordinary arithmetic.

memoryTip: De Morgan: 'break the line, change the sign' — negate each variable, and AND swaps with OR. Then remember absorption kills redundant parentheses.

practice.prompt: Simplify NOT (NOT A AND NOT B).
practice.answer: By De Morgan: NOT (NOT A AND NOT B) = NOT (NOT A) OR NOT (NOT B) = A OR B.

title: From problem to plan: algorithms, flowcharts and pseudocode
objective: Describe the solution to a problem as an ordered algorithm, sketch it as a flowchart and write it precisely in pseudocode.
explanation: Programming logic is the discipline of turning a problem statement into a precise, ordered set of steps — an algorithm — that a computer could execute without asking questions. An algorithm must be finite (it cannot run forever unless that is intended), definite (each step is unambiguous) and produce output. Three interchangeable notations describe one: a flowchart is the visual form, using ovals for start/stop, parallelograms for input/output, rectangles for processing and diamonds for decisions with a branching yes/no path; pseudocode is the text form, written in structured plain English like 'READ number; IF number > 0 THEN PRINT positive ELSE PRINT negative'. Building the habit of writing the plan before the program is what separates reliable coders from trial-and-error typists.
analogy: An algorithm is a recipe: ingredients first (input), exact steps second, and a finished dish third (output). A flowchart is the same recipe photographed as a poster; pseudocode is the same recipe written in clear shorthand. Change the language, never the logic.

workedExamples.title: Algorithm for the larger of two numbers
workedExamples.problem: Write an algorithm that reads two numbers and prints the larger one.
steps: Step 3: IF X > Y THEN PRINT X ELSE PRINT Y.
workedExamples.answer: The plan is finite, ordered and handles both outcomes — a valid algorithm.

workedExamples.title: Flowchart symbols
workedExamples.problem: Which flowchart symbol suits each task: start, read a value, is N > 10?, print total?
steps: A yes/no question -> diamond (decision), with two outgoing arrows labelled Yes and No.

workedExamples.title: Average of three marks
workedExamples.problem: Write pseudocode to read three marks and print their average.
workedExamples.answer: Four pseudocode lines, each one unambiguous action.

rule.title: Algorithm tests
rule.detail: Every algorithm must be finite, definite (no ambiguous steps) and clearly mapped from input to output.

rule.title: Flowchart symbols
rule.detail: Oval = start/stop; parallelogram = input/output; rectangle = process; diamond = decision.

rule.title: Pseudocode keywords
rule.detail: READ/INPUT, PRINT/DISPLAY, SET/<- assignment, IF-THEN-ELSE, WHILE and FOR carry the same meaning in every syllabus.

rule.title: Trace before you trust
rule.detail: Hand-trace your algorithm with a sample input (a dry run) before considering it correct.

mistakes.mistake: Writing steps in an impossible order, such as printing a value before reading it.
mistakes.fix: Follow the data: input -> process -> output.

mistakes.mistake: Mixing pseudocode with real syntax (semicolons, braces, variable declarations).
mistakes.fix: Pseudocode is language-free; keep it in plain structured English.

mistakes.mistake: Leaving a decision branch without an action.
mistakes.fix: Every diamond in a flowchart needs both arrows labelled; every IF needs a defined else behaviour (even if that is 'do nothing', write it).

memoryTip: IPO — Input, Process, Output — is the spine of every algorithm; ovals start, parallelograms read, rectangles compute, diamonds decide.

practice.prompt: Write pseudocode to read a number and print its square.
practice.answer: READ N; SQUARE <- N * N; PRINT SQUARE.

practice.prompt: Which flowchart shape is used for a decision in a flowchart?
practice.answer: A diamond with Yes/No labelled branches.

practice.prompt: What three properties must every algorithm satisfy?
practice.answer: Finiteness, definiteness and clearly defined input/output.

title: Variables, operators and conditional statements
objective: Store values correctly, predict every operator's result (including integer division and precedence) and steer execution with IF/ELSE conditions.
explanation: A variable is a labelled box in memory with three facts: a name, a current value and a data type — integer (whole numbers), float (real numbers), character (single letter enclosed in single quotes), string (text in double quotes) or Boolean (true/false). Operators act on those values: arithmetic operators (+, -, *, /, %) compute; relational operators (<, <=, >, >=, ==, !=) compare and produce a Boolean; logical operators (AND, OR, NOT) combine Booleans. Two results catch most exam questions: integer division throws away the remainder (7 / 2 = 3) while the modulus operator keeps only the remainder (7 % 2 = 1); and precedence means NOT beats AND beats OR, with parentheses overriding everything. Conditional statements (IF, IF-ELSE, ELSE-IF ladders and CASE) choose which block runs based on a Boolean test, so a program can react differently to different inputs rather than always executing the same straight line.
analogy: Variables are labelled boxes on a shelf: the label never changes but the contents can be swapped. Operators are the tools that act on the contents, and an IF-ELSE is a railway junction — the condition is the signal that sends execution down one track or the other.

workedExamples.title: Integer division and modulus
workedExamples.problem: Evaluate 17 / 5 and 17 % 5 under integer arithmetic.
steps: Integer division keeps only the whole quotient: 17 / 5 = 3.

workedExamples.title: Combining conditions
workedExamples.problem: Evaluate (N > 10) AND (N % 2 == 0) when N = 14, then when N = 9.
steps: N = 14: 14 > 10 is true; 14 % 2 == 0 is true; true AND true = true.
N = 9: 9 > 10 is false; 9 % 2 == 0 is false; false AND false = false.
The AND demands both halves to be true.

workedExamples.title: IF-ELSE ladder for grades
workedExamples.problem: Classify a mark M: 80+ = A, 60–79 = B, 40–59 = C, else D.
workedExamples.answer: The ladder checks from the top down, so the first matching branch wins — order matters.

rule.title: Data types
rule.detail: int holds whole numbers, float holds decimals, char holds one character, string holds text, Boolean holds true/false.

rule.title: Division pair
rule.detail: Integer division = quotient only (7/2 -> 3); modulus = remainder only (7%2 -> 1). Even numbers satisfy N % 2 == 0.

rule.title: Precedence
rule.detail: Arithmetic first, then relational, then NOT, then AND, then OR — parentheses override everything.

rule.title: Condition order
rule.detail: In an IF-ELSE ladder arrange tests from most specific to least; equal tests are the classic source of wrong-output bugs.

mistakes.mistake: Using = (assignment) where == (comparison) is meant.
mistakes.fix: = stores a value into a variable; == asks whether two values are equal.

mistakes.mistake: Expecting 7 / 2 to equal 3.5 in integer arithmetic.
mistakes.fix: Integer division discards the fraction; convert to float first if a decimal is needed.

mistakes.mistake: Writing IF M >= 80 ... ELSE IF M > 60 for grades, which hides marks of exactly 60.
mistakes.fix: Use >= with a strict descending ladder so boundary cases such as exactly 60 take the right branch.

memoryTip: '%' remembers what '/' forgets: quotient versus remainder. NOT > AND > OR decides logic precedence.

practice.prompt: What is 123 % 10?
practice.answer: 3 — the last digit, since keep only the remainder of 123 / 10.

practice.prompt: Evaluate NOT (true AND false).
practice.answer: Inside the brackets: true AND false = false; NOT false = true.

title: Loops, tracing and systematic problem solving
objective: Choose and trace the right loop for a task, avoid the classic loop bugs, and apply a repeatable method to unseen output-prediction questions.
explanation: Loops repeat a block of steps. A counted loop (FOR i FROM 1 TO n) is the right form whenever the number of repetitions is known in advance; a WHILE loop runs as long as a condition stays true and suits situations where the count is discovered at run time; a DO-WHILE loop checks the condition after the first pass and therefore always runs at least once. Every loop needs three working parts: an initialisation that starts the control variable, a condition that terminates it, and a body that moves the variable toward termination. With structure in place, problem solving becomes method: restate the problem, fix the input/output contract, outline IPO steps, build a trace table recording every variable on every iteration, then generalize. Output-prediction questions are trace tables in disguise — those who tabulate state never lose track of a value.
analogy: A loop is a washing-machine cycle: set the dial (initialisation), the machine keeps tumbling while the timer is not zero (condition), and each pass uses a little more progress (body); DO-WHILE is the rinse that always runs once even if the timer says stop.

workedExamples.title: Sum with a FOR loop
workedExamples.problem: What does this pseudocode print? S <- 0; FOR i FROM 1 TO 5: S <- S + i; PRINT S.
steps: The loop adds every integer from 1 to 5.
PRINT runs after the loop ends.

workedExamples.title: WHILE with a doubling condition
workedExamples.problem: What does this print? P <- 1; WHILE P <= 10: P <- P * 2. PRINT P.
steps: When P = 16 the condition P <= 10 fails.
The loop exits with P already doubled.

workedExamples.title: Spotting the infinite loop
workedExamples.problem: Why is this wrong? I <- 1; WHILE I != 5: PRINT I; I <- I + 2.
steps: I runs 1, 3, then I = 5: 5 != 5 fails — exit.
Try again with I + 2 from 2: 2, 4, 6, 8 — never equals 5.
The I != 5 condition skips over its own target.
workedExamples.answer: I odd and step 2 always lands on odd numbers; even starts never satisfy I = 5. Use I <= 5 (or I < 6) so the condition can definitely fail.

rule.title: Loop chooser
rule.detail: Known count -> FOR; condition discovered while running -> WHILE; must run at least once -> DO-WHILE.

rule.title: Loop anatomy
rule.detail: Initialise the control variable, test the termination condition, and progress the variable inside the body (i <- i + 1).

rule.title: Trace table
rule.detail: Record every variable's value in every iteration; the last row answers most output-prediction questions.

rule.title: Termination proof
rule.detail: Prefer I <= limit over I != limit so the condition is guaranteed to fail for every possible step size.

mistakes.mistake: Updating the control variable outside the loop body.
mistakes.fix: The increment must execute inside the loop, or the condition never changes and the loop runs forever.

mistakes.mistake: Off-by-one errors such as FOR i FROM 1 TO 10 adding only nine terms or eleven of them.
mistakes.fix: Decide whether the limit is inclusive and trace the final iteration explicitly.

mistakes.mistake: Guessing at compound output instead of tracing.
mistakes.fix: Build the trace table for at least the first three iterations; the pattern then shows itself.

memoryTip: Initialise, test, progress — every loop needs all three. And when in doubt, tabulate: a trace table turns a mystery output into an arithmetic line.

practice.prompt: What does this print? T <- 0; FOR i FROM 1 TO 4: T <- T + i * 2. PRINT T.
Which loop runs its body at least once regardless of the condition?
practice.answer: DO-WHILE, because its condition is checked after the first pass.

practice.prompt: A counter starts at 3 and every pass adds 2; is WHILE C != 8 safe?
practice.answer: No. C runs 3, 5, 7, 9, ... and can never equal 8, so the condition never fails. Use WHILE C <= 8, which stops correctly after C = 9.

title: Days, weeks and reading a clock
objective: Count days and weeks on a calendar, jump weekdays forward with the 7-day cycle and read clock time to the hour and half hour.
explanation: A week is a repeating cycle of 7 weekday names: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday and Sunday. Any question that moves a date forward or backward is settled by dividing the number of days by 7 and using only the remainder. A calendar month shows whole weeks plus a few spare days, which is why a fixed date lands on different weekdays in different months. A clock has a short hour hand and a long minute hand: the minute hand makes one full lap of 60 minutes per hour while the hour hand moves to the next hour mark.
analogy: Think of weekdays as seven seats on a rotating wheel. Whole turns (multiples of 7 days) bring you back to the same seat, so only the leftover days move you to a new seat.

workedExamples.title: Counting days between two dates
workedExamples.problem: How many days are there from 5 March to 21 March?
steps: A subtraction inside the same month gives the gap directly.

workedExamples.title: Weekday after 20 days
workedExamples.problem: Today is Saturday. Which weekday falls 20 days later?
steps: Two whole weeks bring us back to Saturday.
Move 6 seats forward: Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday.

rule.title: Week cycle
rule.detail: There are exactly 7 days in a week; the weekday repeats every 7 days.

rule.title: Remainder rule
rule.detail: The weekday shifts by (number of days mod 7); both directions use the same idea.

rule.title: Weeks and leftover days
rule.detail: n days = floor(n/7) weeks plus n mod 7 leftover days.

rule.title: Clock face
rule.detail: The long hand counts minutes (one lap = 60 minutes); the short hand counts hours (one lap = 12 hours).

mistakes.mistake: Counting 20 days as 20 weekday hops.
mistakes.fix: Only the remainder after dividing by 7 matters: 20 mod 7 = 6.

mistakes.mistake: Counting the first date itself when counting between dates.
mistakes.fix: From 5 to 21 March, the 5th itself is not counted: 21 - 5 = 16 days.

mistakes.mistake: Mixing up the hour hand and minute hand.
mistakes.fix: The hour hand is short and slow; the minute hand is long and makes a full lap every hour.

memoryTip: Whole weeks vanish, leftovers move the weekday; gaps inside a month are simple subtraction.

practice.answer: Saturday. 10 mod 7 = 3; Wednesday plus 3 days is Saturday.

title: Seven-day cycles and clock-face counting
objective: Work with seven-day weekday cycles, identify leap years and count angles swept by clock hands in simple cases.
explanation: Weekdays repeat every 7 days, so any date-offset question reduces to the remainder of the number of days on division by 7. A common year has 365 = 52 x 7 + 1 days, contributing one odd day, and a leap year has 366, contributing two. A year is leap when it is divisible by 4, except century years, which must be divisible by 400. On a clock face the minute hand covers 360 degrees in 60 minutes and the hour hand covers 30 degrees per hour, so at h o'clock sharp the hands form |30h| degrees or its supplement to 360.
analogy: Weekdays rotate like a Ferris wheel with exactly seven cabins: after any number of full revolutions only the remainder seat tells you where you stop.

workedExamples.title: Counting days forward
workedExamples.problem: Today is Thursday. Which day falls 15 days later?

workedExamples.title: Leap-year test
workedExamples.problem: Which of 1900, 2000 and 2024 are leap years?
steps: 2024 is divisible by 4 and not a century year, so it is leap.
1900 is a century year not divisible by 400, so it is not leap.
2000 is a century year divisible by 400, so it is leap.
workedExamples.answer: 2000 and 2024 are leap years; 1900 is not.

rule.title: Weekday modulo
rule.detail: Weekday shift = number of days mod 7.

rule.title: Odd days
rule.detail: Common year: 1 odd day; leap year: 2 odd days.

rule.title: Leap rule
rule.detail: Leap = divisible by 4, but century years need divisibility by 400.

rule.title: Clock basics
rule.detail: Minute hand: 6 degrees per minute; hour hand: 30 degrees per hour; at h:00 the angle is 30h (or 360 - 30h).

mistakes.mistake: Calling 1900 a leap year.
mistakes.fix: Century years leap only when divisible by 400: 1600, 2000 leap; 1700, 1800, 1900 do not.

mistakes.mistake: Adding 15 days and answering two weekdays ahead.
mistakes.fix: 15 mod 7 = 1, so only one weekday forward.

mistakes.mistake: Confusing hour-hand speed as 6 degrees per minute.
mistakes.fix: 6 degrees per minute belongs to the minute hand; the hour hand moves half a degree per minute.

memoryTip: Mod 7 moves weekdays, +1 odd day per common year, +2 for leap, and century leaps need 400.

title: Odd-day books, century maths and clock coincidences
objective: Accumulate odd days across years and centuries, compute weekday jumps between two dates and use the 65 5/11-minute coincidence rule.
explanation: Weekday arithmetic runs on odd days: each common year contributes 1 and each leap year 2, so 100 years (76 common + 24 leap) give 76 + 48 = 124 odd days, and 124 mod 7 = 5; a 400-year block cycles to 0. The minutes hand and hour hand coincide every 65 5/11 minutes, because the hour hand gains 55 minutes on the dial each 60-minute hour: 60 x 12/11 = 65 5/11. The angle between hands at h hours m minutes is |30h - 5.5m| degrees, reduced to the smaller angle.
analogy: Odd days are pockets of spare change: every year leaves one or two coins, 100 years leave five coins on the table, and only full centuries of 400 cancel the whole tab.

workedExamples.title: Odd days in 100 years
workedExamples.problem: How many odd days does a block of 100 ordinary years contain?
workedExamples.answer: 124 odd days, which is 5 weekdays' worth.

workedExamples.title: Hands coinciding
workedExamples.problem: Between 3 and 4 o'clock, at what time do the hands coincide?
steps: The hands coincide at m = 60h/11 minutes past h.

rule.title: Date jump
rule.detail: Days between two dates mod 7 gives the weekday shift.

rule.title: Coincidence spacing
rule.detail: The hands coincide every 65 5/11 minutes; 11 coincidences in 12 hours.

rule.title: Angle formula
rule.detail: Angle = |30h - 5.5m|; reduce to at most 180.

mistakes.mistake: Counting the endpoint year as leap wrongly in century blocks.
mistakes.fix: Use the fixed decomposition: 100 years = 76 common + 24 leap.

mistakes.mistake: Stating the hands coincide every 65 minutes exactly.
mistakes.fix: The exact spacing is 65 5/11 minutes; 11 meets fit in 12 hours.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting to reduce an angle over 180 degrees.
mistakes.fix: Angles between hands report the smaller of the two.

memoryTip: Pockets: 1, 2 per years; 100-year pockets are 5; hands meet 11 times per 12 hours spaced 65 5/11 minutes apart.
